94f76cbd411e0ba1: KUALA LUMPUR, Nov 16 — Two former senior executives of a construction company pleaded not guilty at the Sessions Court here today to three amended charges of criminal breach of trust (CBT) and abetment involving RM72,000 in penalty proceeds for a proposed office complex in Putrajaya.

Former THP Bina Sdn Bhd health and safety manager Nasahruddin Ahmad, 56, and former TH Properties Sdn Bhd deputy general manager Tengku Kamarolhisham Tengku Kamaruddin, 55, who also served as THP Bina Sdn Bhd deputy general manager, entered their pleas after the charges were read out before Judge Rosli Ahmad.
THP Bina Sdn Bhd is a wholly-owned subsidiary of TH Properties Sdn Bhd, a subsidiary of Lembaga Tabung Haji, that focuses on construction and project management.
Earlier, Deputy Public Prosecutor Irna Julieza Maaras told the court that the three charges against both men had been amended.
The amendments involved replacing the phrase “by depositing the money into Nasahruddin’s account” with “by not handing over the money to THP Bina Sdn Bhd” across all three charges.

According to the amended charges, Nasahruddin, in his capacity as the company’s health and safety manager, was entrusted with RM72,000 in penalty proceeds collected from contractor Fourth Wave Sdn Bhd. He is accused of committing CBT by not handing over the money to THP Bina Sdn Bhd.

The penalty proceeds were linked to the proposed development of an office complex in Precinct 3, Federal Territory of Putrajaya, comprising several office floors in Blocks A, B, C and D, an auditorium, and an underground car park for THP Bina Sdn Bhd.

He allegedly committed the offences at Kompleks Islam Putrajaya in Precinct 3 between April 26, 2013, and Aug 12, 2015. The charges, framed under Section 409 of the Penal Code, carry a maximum sentence of 20 years’ imprisonment, whipping, and a fine upon conviction.

Meanwhile, Tengku Kamarolhisham faced three amended charges of abetting Nasahruddin by instructing him not to hand over the money to THP Bina Sdn Bhd at the same place and time. The charges were framed under Section 109 of the Penal Code, read together with Section 409 of the same code.
Lawyer Fahmi Abd Moin represented both accused during today’s proceedings, while the court set Dec 17 for mention to submit documents. — Bernama
eb542aa8402d76b1: GENEVA, Nov 16 — The spread of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) is threatening modern medicine despite progress in combating drug-resistant bacteria, senior World Health Organisation officials said today.
WHO officials said countries had expanded efforts to tackle AMR, but warned that progress in prevention, diagnosis and the appropriate use of antibiotics remained too slow to meet global targets.
Bacteria have long evolved resistance to medicines designed to kill them.
The widespread use of antibiotics in human health, animal husbandry and food production has accelerated the problem, making AMR one of the leading causes of infectious-disease deaths worldwide.
“Antimicrobial resistance is widespread and threatening the future of modern medicine,” said Jean-Pierre Nyemazi, interim head of antimicrobial resistance at the WHO.
“Unlike Covid-19, which was very visible, drug-resistant infections have been taking people’s lives for years without us noticing it and raising the alarm as we should,” said Nyemazi.
In 2021 alone, AMR was directly responsible for more than one million deaths and linked to some 4.7 million others, said the agency.

A WHO investigation in 183 countries into the progress of the fight against antimicrobial resistance this year revealed that nearly nine countries in 10 had a national action plan against the phenomenon. In 2017, the figure was only around four in 10.
But only 42 countries — less than one in five — said they had a plan that was financed, implemented and monitored, said Pravasha Prakash, an AMR technical officer with the global health agency.
“Countries are moving forward in every step but progress still needs to be speeded up to reach the 2030 targets,” she added.
Poor access to diagnostics

One of the main weaknesses remains access to diagnostics. Only 36 per cent of countries had a national reference laboratory capable of testing for resistance in all bacteria and fungi monitored by the WHO—well short of the 80 per cent target set for 2030.
“Without testing, clinicians must treat without knowing the cause of infection or which antibiotic will work,” said Sylvia Bertagnolo, head of surveillance for AMR at the WHO.
The latest global surveillance data show that in 2023, one in every six laboratory-confirmed bacterial infections flagged to the WHO was resistant to antibiotics used to treat it.
As a result, the WHO has announced the release of two new tools designed to help countries strengthen their diagnostic capacities.
The first defines the tests that should be available at every level of the healthcare system, from primary care centres to referral hospitals.
The second compiles 73 laboratory procedures, from sample collection to the identification of pathogens and antibiotic susceptibility testing.
The WHO has estimated that AMR could cause some 39 million deaths between now and 2050.
There needed to be improved use of existing antibiotics, at a time when the development of new treatments is failing to keep pace with the rise of resistance, it said.
Infection prevention, vaccination, improved access to water and sanitation, and the appropriate use of antimicrobials are the main levers to combat the issue, it added. — AFP
3b9a13a4cbf04610: MOSCOW: Ukraine fired hundreds of drones at Russia overnight, aiming towards Moscow and hitting a symbolic bridge that links the annexed Crimean peninsula to Russia.
The strike on the bridge appeared to inflict only minor damage, though it drew an angry response from Russian-installed officials.

Ukraine launched 1,336 drones in the barrage, Moscow's defence ministry said in a statement – the second-highest daily figure so far this year, according to an AFP tally of official Russian statements.

The barrage came days before a summit in Shenzhen between President Vladimir Putin, US President Donald Trump and Chinese President Xi Jinping. US officials say Russia's war against Ukraine is not expected to be a focus of the talks.
"The enemy has hit the Crimea bridge," Crimean's Russian-installed governor Sergey Aksyonov wrote on Telegram. "As a result, traffic will be restricted, likely until the afternoon."
He did not say whether anyone was killed or wounded in the strike. Social media channels close to the Russian army indicated no serious damage had been sustained in the attack.
The bridge has been a key target for Ukraine since Russia launched its offensive in February 2022.
It has been struck several times, including an October 2022 blast in which an explosive-packed truck was detonated on the bridge, causing months of disruption.
Around 600 of the drones were intercepted on approach to the Russian capital, Moscow Mayor Sergei Sobyanin said.
The interceptions came hours after Ukrainian forces struck a major Russian petrochemical plant, an oil refinery and a military production site.

Kyiv says its retaliatory strikes are justified retribution for Moscow's own missile and drone barrages of its cities and energy grid – attacks that have killed hundreds of civilians and regularly knock out power and heating for millions.
'World peace'
Diplomatic efforts to end the almost five-year war have so far gone nowhere.

After a fresh round of talks in Abu Dhabi last week, Russian President Vladimir Putin reiterated his hardline territorial demands and said any deployment of foreign troops would be seen in Moscow as a "continuation of war."
Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky said the US had proposed Kyiv ceding some territory in exchange for being given Nato membership.
Moscow has repeatedly said it will not accept Ukraine being admitted to the US-led alliance.
Against that backdrop, China confirmed on Monday that Xi would hold talks with Trump and Putin in Shenzhen on November 19 on the sidelines of the Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation (Apec) summit.
The Kremlin and White House had previously confirmed the meeting.
Beijing said the trio would discuss "world peace".
Trump has said he intends to discuss denuclearisation and the Iran war.
He is not expected to discuss Russia's war against Ukraine in the trilateral talks, according to US officials.

Zelensky has warned that the Shenzhen meeting risks becoming a 21st-century version of the 1945 Yalta conference, where major powers could attempt to redraw spheres of influence without smaller countries at the table.
a7623fa46c90cf7a: Officials claim the measure ‘protects society,’ but civil society organizations see a threat to freedom of expression
Originally published on Global Voices
Post-election protests in Maputo, Mozambique, in 2025. Photo by Wilson Thole. Used with permission.

Civil society organizations in Mozambique, such as the Center for Democracy and Human Rights (CDD), submitted a document to the Ombudsman contesting the constitutionality of Decree No. 48/2025, issued in December 2025, which establishes control mechanisms and potential blocks on access to telecommunications networks in the country.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

According to the portal Moz24h, journalists and experts are concerned that the measure could threaten rights such as freedom of expression, access to information, and communication, particularly in contexts of social mobilization or political tension. The challenge arises in an environment still heated from the conflicts following the 2024 elections.

Activists and civil society actors argue that the decree could enable restrictions on access to the internet and digital platforms — tools that have become increasingly central to the circulation of information, the organization of protests, and civic participation. The approved text allows the state to suspend telecommunications services for up to 48 hours without needing a court order, reports Deutsche Welle.

Also, according to civil society organizations, the decree grants broad powers to authorities to intervene in telecommunications networks on grounds of national security or the maintenance of public order.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

By appealing to the Ombudsman, the organizations are requesting an analysis of whether the decree is compatible with the Constitution of the Republic of Mozambique, as well as Mozambique’s international commitments regarding human rights and freedom of expression.

In March 2026, the Minister of Communications and Digital Transformation, Américo Muchanga, denied that the measure restricted rights. He defended it as a way to protect society in critical moments, strengthening the state’s capacity to manage crises and protect critical telecommunications infrastructure.
Experts diverge in their reading
In discussions with Global Voices, various experts presented different interpretations of its potential impacts.

One researcher, who asked not to be identified for security reasons, recalls that several democracies around the world have legal mechanisms allowing temporary restrictions on communications. For the researcher, political contexts where social demonstrations are frequently interpreted as threats to stability can make the application of this type of legislation particularly sensitive. He notes:

O que foi feito neste decreto é tentativa de legalizar toda e qualquer ação que o governo possa ter em uma situação de protesto social. Na França existe, no Brasil existe, nos Estados Unidos existem. Em qualquer parte em que exista alguma democracia, que chamamos a dita democracia consolidada, existem dispositivos estatais, governamentais, que limitam o acesso às comunicações, quando se entende que eles violam o direito de outras pessoas ou imposições em causa do próprio Estado. Não é o decreto o problema. O problema é como pode ser aplicado. O nosso problema é que não há tolerância. Tudo aquilo que parece ser protesto é visto como tentativa de subversão, tentativa de colocar em causa a ordem. É um problema histórico de governança e questão central na interpretação também do próprio decreto.

What was done in this decree is an attempt to legalize any and all actions the government might take in a situation of social protest. It exists in France, it exists in Brazil, and it exists in the United States. Anywhere there is some form of democracy, what we call so-called consolidated democracies, there are state, governmental mechanisms that limit access to communications when it is understood that they violate the rights of other people or impose demands against the state itself. The decree is not the problem. The problem is how it can be applied. Our problem is that there is no tolerance. Everything that looks like a protest is seen as an attempt at subversion, an attempt to jeopardize order. It is a historical problem of governance and a central issue in the interpretation of the decree itself.

Meanwhile, activist and journalist Nadio Taimo emphasizes that the decree comes at a time when Mozambique’s digital civic spaces face growing pressure. According to him, internet access has become fundamental for the circulation of information and the exercise of freedom of expression. Taimo observes that many media outlets migrated to digital platforms because of the high costs of traditional printing, making the online environment an important space for news dissemination, public debate, and social mobilization. In this context, potential blocks on internet access could significantly limit access to information.

Já temos uma expansão, uma onda crescente de jornais eletrônicos. Já não imprimimos jornais, devido aos custos. Migramos para a era digital, logo, há aqui um bloqueio de acesso à informação, e até o próprio espaço de opinião, de promoção da liberdade de expressão, pode ser limitado. Os órgãos de comunicação social são todos, a maior parte deles, do governo, e controlados, e nos é fechado o espaço cívico, o espaço físico, nas ruas, quando nos proíbem de realizar marchas.

We already have an expansion: a growing wave of electronic newspapers. We no longer print newspapers due to costs. We migrated to the digital era; therefore, there is a block on access to information here, and even the very space for opinion, for promoting freedom of expression, can be limited. The media outlets are all — most of them — government-owned and controlled, and our civic space, the physical space in the streets, is closed to us when they prohibit us from holding marches.
The activist further adds that the decree could formalize practices that, according to civil society organizations, have already occurred during moments of political tension:
Este documento é apenas uma formalização de uma intenção política de bloqueio da internet, que já vinha sendo aplicada, só que não havia uma formalização legal.
This document is merely a formalization of a political intention to block the internet, which was already being applied, only without a legal framework.
Precedent cases: Protests and control

The debate over telecommunications control in Mozambique is also linked to previous episodes of social mobilization. In February 2008 and September 2010, mass protests in the cities of Maputo and Matola were triggered by the rising cost of living, particularly the prices of transport and essential goods. During those demonstrations, mobile phones and text messages were widely used to mobilize and coordinate actions. In response, the government at the time promoted stricter communications regulation measures, including mandatory SIM card registration for all users.

New protests broke out again in November 2012 as young people protested the fare hikes for urban semi-collective transport, locally known as chapa-100. Swift intervention by police forces in areas with the highest concentration of protesters prevented the demonstrations from spreading.

These episodes occurred during defining moments of social demand by Mozambican youth in the post-independence period (1975), reflecting frustrations over economic inequalities, unemployment, and the rising cost of living amid economic liberalization. In this scenario, urban culture also played an important role in expressing social discontent. Artists like the rapper Azagaia became influential voices among young people, with social critique songs widely broadcast during demonstrations and across digital platforms.
A regional trend of internet shutdowns

The debate in Mozambique is not an isolated situation. International digital monitoring organizations have documented numerous cases of internet shutdowns in African countries in recent years, often linked to electoral processes, popular protests, or internal conflicts. In Angola and Guinea-Bissau, for instance, blocking or restricting internet access has been utilized by governments during periods of political instability.<!--TgQPHd|||[]-->

Human rights organizations and digital freedom advocacy groups argue that shutdowns limit access to information, hinder the work of journalists, and restrict civic participation, while digital governance experts warn that such measures can have significant impacts not only on public debate, but also on the livelihoods of the civilian population.

Despite the ratification of the aforementioned decree in Mozambique, its practical application has not yet been documented, making it difficult to assess its potential effects in practice. Concurrently, the Constitutional Council has not yet ruled on civil society organizations’ position regarding the decree’s potential unconstitutionality, contributing to a landscape of legal and institutional uncertainty.

f352c897b2108aac: PETALING JAYA, Nov 16 — University students could get help exploring careers, finding internships and preparing for job interviews from their first year through Talentbank’s Career Passport platform.
In a statement today, Talentbank said the initiative aims to help students understand what employers expect and prepare for working life throughout their studies.

“Our hope is that every young Malaysian, wherever they study, will have a companion for their career, from the day they start university to their first job and through a lifetime of learning,” its founder and chief executive officer Ben Ho said.

The platform is designed to bring together job and internship listings, interview practice, alumni connections and job matching, giving students access to opportunities beyond employers that visit their own university.
It also aims to connect students with thousands of verified mentors from leading companies for advice on career paths and the skills employers value.
University career centres would be able to track students’ progress and identify those who need support earlier, while employers could engage with potential recruits before graduation.

The initiative forms part of a collaboration involving the Higher Education Ministry, universities, business associations, chambers and Talentbank, which signed and exchanged memoranda of understanding at the ninth Graduates’ Choice Award gala at Sunway Resort on November 13.

Dari segi infrastruktur, sembilan Kolam Takungan Setempat (OSD) telah siap dibina manakala enam lagi sedang dalam pembinaan dan tambahan enam lagi dirancang pada 2027.

f9f093684b1a4af4: If you've made mistakes at work that threatened to torch your career, The Register has just the column for you. We call it Who, Me?, we print one every Monday, and you're reading this week's instalment!
Today, meet a reader we'll Regomize as "Axl" who once worked at a petrol station (aka a gas station for US readers).
One Friday afternoon, in the shadow of a holiday weekend, the PC that drove the station's pumps and point of sale stopped working, leaving it unable to operate.
Axl called the manufacturer and got the very unwelcome news that a technician could visit on Tuesday at the earliest.
As the petrol station was in a spot that would attract a few weekend tourists, the potential losses were substantial, and Axl felt he needed to act.

He knew the main computer lived inside a large metal box affixed to a wall, an arrangement that meant electronics and flammable vapors were always kept well apart. The machine's power switch was accessible, so Axl turned it off and on again – and watched the machine come back to life, before shutting itself down five minutes later.

That behavior was a strong hint that something was overheating but confirming that theory was not easy because the metal case included a lock (see previous remarks about preventing fires) and Axl didn't have they key.
Axl inspected the hinges on the box, found they were held on with screws and was able to remove the lid and access the PC.
"Aside from the considerable amount of dust and hair inside, I could see that the CPU fan was not turning," he wrote. "Either it had failed or was not receiving the control signal to cool."
The service station had an office out the back. Axl liberated a desk fan, pointed it at the PC, and watched it come alive again.
An hour later, the PC was still working, so Axl decided he needed a fix that would last the weekend.

"I drove to a local electrical shop and purchased a high speed bathroom extraction fan which I rigged up inside the case, then closed it up best I could with tape and cardboard," he told The Register.
That rickety rig kept fuel flowing for three days.

"On Tuesday afternoon, the support engineer arrived and I explained how I kept us in business over the weekend," Axl wrote. "He just shrugged his shoulders, smiled and changed the failed fan. I didn't even get the 'It's our kit, leave it alone' lecture."
He did get the satisfaction of a job well done.
"No one died from an exploding petrol station and the tourists were happy they could go home," he wrote.

2c711f21a3b1d02f: Microsoft has issued version 4.0 of its very own Azure Linux, which it built atop Fedora for the first time and now suggests is ready to run mainstream workloads.

Redmond’s history with Linux is long and tangled. Former CEO Steve Ballmer infamously labelled the project a cancer but by 2015 Microsoft had quietly adapted the OS to power some switches in its Azure Cloud.

Microsoft then built some of its own Azure services on containers and created a lightweight Linux for them to run in. In 2020, Microsoft released that Linux as CBL-Mariner, largely so that developers who used services like Azure Kubernetes Service (AKS) that relied on the OS could access the platform they were building for.
In 2022, CBL-Mariner became Azure Linux 2.0, another container-centric lightweight release. Version 3.0 followed in 2024, now billed as ready for “broad Azure usage” with Azure Kubernetes Service.

In June 2026, Microsoft announced version 4.0 and billed it as suitable for Azure Virtual Machines, VM Scale Sets, and container images. The big change that made that repositioning possible was basing the OS on Fedora rather than Microsoft’s own Common Base Linux.

Microsoft also tuned the Linux kernel – version 6.18 LTS – by adding Hyper-V guest drivers and other features that make it behave well in Azure. It also natively supports tools like Microsoft Defender for Cloud, Azure Monitor, and the Azure CLI, which Microsoft reckons committed Azure users already employ and therefore want to apply to their cloudy Linux workloads.
Or as Redmond puts it: “the familiarity of [the] RPM package ecosystem, while adding Azure-native security, compliance, and operational capabilities.”
All of those changes add up to an OS that Microsoft says is worth a look “Whether you're running web applications, databases, or GPU-accelerated AI/ML workloads.”

Redmond makes that recommendation in part because Azure Linux comes with “no additional OS licensing cost.” Other commercial Linux distributions will cost users money, meaning Microsoft can now make an argument that SUSE and RHEL subscriptions might be superfluous for both AKS users and those who use Azure to host other applications on Linux.
Azure Linux 4.0 debuted last Thursday and is available here. Redmond’s latest Linux debuted just days after Microsoft issued a monster upgrade to version 3.0. ®

5b065f5caeea076e: WASHINGTON: The weekend US air traffic outage ranks as the worst in 35 years for flight cancellations caused by a technology issue, surpassing Southwest Airlines’s 2022 systems meltdown, according to travel app Flighty.

With every US carrier affected by the four-hour nationwide stoppage on Friday, the number of flight cancellations had exceed 17,000 by Sunday, aviation data providers including Flighty and Cirium said. That surpassed the 16,900 scrapped flights caused by Southwest’s tech troubles in the winter holiday of 2022.

Airlines and passengers are still reeling from the days of disruption caused by only the third nationwide ground-stop in history, and the worst since the September 2001 terror attacks. The issue has been traced to the replacement of outdated copper wire at a remote location in Arkansas and a router that started flooding the air-traffic control system with connection attempts.

Cancellations started to ease on Sunday, with more than 2,220 flights affected as of 11.15pm New York time, according to FlightAware data, though more than 10,100 services were delayed as airlines struggled to get planes and crew back on schedule.
Major airlines including Delta Air Lines and Alaska Air Group said they are anticipating a more normal service or vastly reduced cancelations Monday.

So far, American Airlines Group is the most-impacted airline by total, with more than 5,300 services scrapped since Friday, while financially-troubled JetBlue Airways was the worst hit as a proportion of flights, according to flight data provider Cirium.

The latest air traffic tech troubles also surpassed major crises like the 2024 global IT failure of CrowdStrike Holdings, which grounded flights and impacted businesses around the world. The CrowdStrike chaos triggered a further crisis for Delta at the time, after its crew-scheduling system failed.

428730d65d2647f0: On November 14, Asia fired up its wind machines and pyrotechnics for the inaugural Eurovision Song Contest Asia, aka Eurovision Asia. Eleven countries competed – from Bangladesh and Bhutan to Vietnam and host country Thailand. Notably absent this first year were most of the continent’s most populous nations: China, India, Japan, Pakistan and Indonesia. The format was familiar: three-minute songs performed with no more than six people permitted on stage. But there was a distinct regional inflection in the staging, costuming and language choices. Regional flavour Many of the artists wove in elements of traditional sound and traditional dress, and artists expressed gratitude to the audience with the traditional Thai gesture wai (hands together). While the original Eurovision is hosted in a combination of English and French, Eurovision Asia was delivered in English only. But most artists performed either in their own language (36%) or a combination of that language with English (54%). Only South Korea’s song was performed entirely in English. By comparison, Eurovision 2026 featured 43% of songs entirely in English, 38% in languages other than English, and 19% multilingual. Musically, it was a diverse offering. The delicate lotus leaves of Vietnam’s Tóc Tiên and her back-up dancers broke into a high-energy opening number, Em Tiên. Malaysia’s Aina Abdul finished the show with a pitch-perfect power ballad, Bluest Sky. In between, audiences were treated to Cambodian and Bhutanese ballads, Bengali a capella, South Korean K-pop and, perhaps most surprisingly, Nepali rock. Girls to the front But it was the Philippines’ Carmelle – the youngest contestant, at 19 – who won the night with Sobra-Sobra. The focus of the empowering pop song in English and Tagalog was about Filipino women’s right to be who they want to be. “It’s about how unapologetic, independent and strong Filipinas are. It describes me – not just me, but of course all the Filipinas,” Carmelle told The Guardian. Carmelle received 211 points, winning both the jury and the public vote, encompassing viewers from 183 countries and territories. With her victory, the Philippines has won the right to host Eurovision Asia in 2027. In the meantime, Carmelle will also perform at the 2027 Eurovision Song Contest in Bulgaria. Carmelle rehearsing Sobra-Sobra at the Eurovision Song Contest Asia. Eurovision Song Contest Asia Spectacle and snags Eurovision is known for its spectacle, and Eurovision Asia delivered, albeit on a more modest budget. Stage production made the most of stunning visual projections, smoke and flares. Eurovision is also known for its non-political stance, with political or ideological messages prohibited. But it has been more forgiving toward humanitarian statements. And at Eurovision Asia, Nepal’s Pratik Himal Rai used the end of his set to call for support for his country as it recovers from the August flood disaster. The show was not without its hitches. Laos’ representative, Thinla, couldn’t hear her music due to an issue with her earpiece, so footage of her technical rehearsal was shown at the end of the performances to ensure fair judgement of her act. Thai artists Mang x Daou experienced wardrobe malfunctions during their ballad Aroma, though this didn’t affect their chances in the voting – Thailand came in second place, with 169 points. Why not Asiavision? If Europe has Eurovision, why can’t Asia have Asiavision? For one, the name “Asiavision” is already taken: it’s the broadcasting network of the Asia-Pacific Broadcasting Union (ABU), which has its own song contests and festivals. But mostly, it’s about branding. Although the name Eurovision has become synonymous with the song contest, it actually refers to the European Broadcasting Union’s (EBU) pan-European telecommunications network. The Eurovision Song Contest was created in 1956 to promote the network and attract audiences across borders. (No, it was not created to unite a war-torn Europe.) The purpose of Eurovision Asia is specifically to expand the Eurovision brand and format into the region. This is a project the EBU has been attempting for more than two decades. It plans to continue the expansion of the brand through other continental editions. MANG x DAOU rehearsing for Thailand at Eurovision Song Contest Asia in Bangkok. Ralph Larmann/Eurovision The future of Eurovision Asia Staging the inaugural competition is one thing, but securing the longevity of the franchise in Asia is another matter. Buy-in from economic powerhouses Japan, China and India may be the key to its success. Negotiations were underway with China and Japan to participate this year, and organisers are optimistic that they and several others will join in 2027. The broad geographical scope of “Asia” also has the potential to draw in participants from the Middle East. But broader participation presents its own challenges. The original Eurovision is heavily associated with LGBTQIA+ acceptance and pride, which may not be well-received by certain broadcasters and their audiences within Asia. We saw this play out in the inaugural Eurovision Asia contest: Malaysian broadcaster TV3 cut drag performer Vice Ganda, the Phillipines’ jury spokesperson, from its broadcast. There was also speculation about whether Islamophobia played a role in Malaysia’s Aina Abdul’s results; despite being a favourite to win going into the contest, she finished in fourth place. Soft power and pop Like the OG Eurovision, Eurovision Asia offers great potential for soft power politics. It also has the potential to be a powerful global platform for Asian pop. The inaugural competition was a diverse showcase for the unique voices and cultures of its participants, beyond the dominant trends of J- and K-pop. Hopefully we will get a chance to see more in Manila next year. 279fed26f5857518: HONG KONG: A resounding Democratic takeover of Capitol Hill did more than rattle Asian chipmakers.
It set off a macro realignment of foreign policy, energy, and trade that could create new winners and losers across Asian markets.
The "blue wave" in the US midterm elections on Nov 3 triggered an anti-AI market shock, sending the tech-heavy Nasdaq to its steepest fall in 19 months.
Investors feared that incoming Democratic leaders would subject AI companies to stricter scrutiny, including over data centre construction and tax breaks.
Asian equities — home to some of the world's biggest chipmakers — led the regional retreat in the week of the vote.
South Korea's KOSPI and Taiwan's TAIEX each tumbled 12%, dragging the broader MSCI Asia ex Japan index down 5%.

While Asian markets have recovered some ground, investors remain on edge after an October tech selloff driven by valuation concerns and doubts about the payoff from AI investment, fears since amplified by turmoil at Nvidia, a key engine of the AI boom.
The risk from the AI blowback is clearly concentrated in North Asia.
The CSOP-Solactive AI exchange-traded fund, the region's leading AI-focused fund, allocates 37% to Taiwan and South Korea and 26% to Japan.
KraneShares' more geographically diversified AI ETF allocates 12% to China, highlighting Asia's wide exposure to the sector.

Less tech-dependent neighbours are feeling less heat from the AI jitters. India's benchmark BSE Sensex rose 7% in the election week, while Singapore's Straits Times Index fell only 3%; both have since advanced further.
If the tech rout deepens, these markets appear better placed than the regional bourses that led gains in the first half of 2026.
Competing forges
The ramifications of the US elections for Asia extend well beyond data centres.
First, there is US policy in the Middle East. Democratic congressional control could pressure the White House to de-escalate the US-Iran war.
Indeed, president Donald Trump said that the US was unlikely to strike Iran while negotiations continued, a far cry from the more hawkish rhetoric before the elections.
Markets appear to be pricing in this policy shift. Since the midterms, benchmark Brent crude oil has fallen for a second straight week, dropping nearly 19% to below US$96 a barrel.

Cheaper energy could offer relief across Asia. Historically, around 80% of oil and 90% of gas transiting the Strait of Hormuz chokepoint were destined for ‌Asian markets, meaning this year’s Middle East conflict, which effectively closed the narrow waterway for months, has hit the region particularly hard.
The countries that stand to benefit the most from falling fuel prices include Japan, South Korea and India.

In addition to weighing on inflation and helping boost growth, declining oil prices should also be positive for Asian energy importers' trade balances, which, all else being equal, could help boost their currencies.
However, this is where countries may see greater divergence.

North Asian economies have seen their trade surpluses balloon over the past year on the back of massive AI exports. So, if oil prices and AI demand decline together, the latter could offset the former, leaving large tech exporters as net losers. That shouldn't be the case for their less tech-exposed neighbours.

Currency markets illustrate the divide. Since Nov 3, South Korea's won and the Taiwan dollar have underperformed their major Asian peers, whereas the Indian rupee, heavily exposed to oil prices but not to tech hardware exports, has appreciated sharply.
Affordability push

A widely held view in the US, echoed by leaders on both sides of the aisle, is that elevated prices were a major factor behind the Democratic landslide. Policy focused on improving affordability could therefore become more prominent in both parties' agendas.

Tariffs played a role in cost-of-living concerns, so the election results may reduce the likelihood that Trump ratchets up his aggressive trade policy, even if he could persist via executive authority.
Given bipartisan concerns about China, trade pressure on Beijing may not ease.
However, this could benefit other Asian countries that supply consumer goods, such as Vietnam, Bangladesh, Thailand, Indonesia and India.
Another key affordability issue was healthcare. Efforts by Democrats to lower healthcare costs could accelerate demand for generic drugs and outsourced manufacturing.

India could be well positioned here. The country’s generic manufacturers, including Sun Pharmaceutical Industries, produce roughly 20% of the world's generic medicines and already supply about 40% of US demand for generics.
Another winner could be contract development and manufacturing organisations (CDMOs) such as South Korea's Samsung Biologics, which provide outsourced manufacturing services to major US drugmakers.
When tailwinds converge
India appears to be the Asian market that most clearly ticks all of the above boxes.
As a net energy importer with minimal exposure to tech cycles, it could directly capture the upside of lower commodity prices, reduced trade pressure and pharmaceutical tailwinds.
It was therefore no surprise that Indian stocks outperformed after the vote.
Foreign flows have also skyrocketed in recent days, underscoring investors’ renewed confidence in a market often touted as an “anti-AI” play.
However, nothing is certain.
Should Trump leverage his executive powers to escalate Middle East conflicts, any projected relief from inflation or high energy costs would immediately vanish.
He could also shrug off voter concerns and continue to pursue his aggressive tariff agenda.

Furthermore, if strategic competition with China pushes Washington to loosen domestic constraints on AI development, capital could pivot rapidly back to North Asian hardware exporters, relegating markets like India to the sidelines.
For now, navigating Asia requires recognising that Washington's policy shifts reach far beyond the AI supply chain.
(The views expressed here are those of Manishi Raychaudhuri, the founder and CEO of Emmer Capital Partners Ltd and the former head of Asia-Pacific Equity Research at BNP Paribas Securities.)

Alongside the SpaceX chief, the tech heavyweight signatories include Tim Sweeney, founder and CEO of video game publisher Epic Games, and Garry Tan, president of Y Combinator, San Francisco’s most renowned business incubator.

Another signatory, Uber co-founder Travis Kalanick, wrote that Huang had “erred, yes — to err is to be human — but I do not believe anything he has done rises to the bar of separating him from his company.”
More than 7,500 signatories identify themselves as Nvidia employees, equivalent to 18 per cent of the company’s workforce.
The support illustrates the unique standing of the leather-jacketed executive, who is seen as a godfather of AI within the industry.
Under his leadership, Nvidia became a pivotal Silicon Valley investor, financing data centres and startups, earning it the nickname “the central bank of AI.”
But the company has also faced criticism that it has fuelled a speculative investment bubble.
Huang championed open AI models, including Chinese ones, and fought any constraints on the AI race, clashing on these issues with Claude creator Anthropic and its chief Dario Amodei.

On Friday, two major shareholders, investors Brad Gerstner and Gavin Baker, urged the board to keep “all options” open.

“They need a dramatic shake-up,” Bessent said on Fox News, demanding that the company explain whether it had knowingly turned a blind eye to the smuggling of its chips to China. — AFP
e1b19cda99281fde: SYDNEY: Australia on Monday expressed concern its economy will take a hit from "manipulation" of trade in its biggest export iron ore, by its biggest customer China.
The world's top producer, Australia exported 944 million tonnes of iron ore last year, of which three-quarters were shipped to China for steel making.

The trade has withstood political disputes between the two countries, flowing even as China imposed blocks on A$20 billion (US$13.5 billion) worth of Australian coal, wine and agricultural exports in 2020 as retaliation for Canberra's call for an inquiry into the origins of Covid-19.
But China's formation of a central buying body to lower the price its steel makers pay Australian iron ore producers risks souring trade.
China's embassy did not respond to a request for comment.

Resources minister Madeleine King said on Monday the activity of China Minerals Resources Group, which has reportedly sought to block sales by Australian producers as it negotiates contracts, was against the international rules of trade.
"The export of iron ore from this country since it started in the 60s has been integral to our national economy," King told national broadcaster ABC.

"When there is movements by the biggest consumer of that product to moderate the prices in their favour, well, that is of concern to the government because it affects the budget bottom line," she said.
"The manipulation of trade is not good for our country," she added.
The government has previously said iron ore negotiations were a commercial matter.
King said on Monday she is in discussions with Australia's iron ore producers.
CMRG was formed in 2022 to centralise buying. China is the world's biggest buyer of iron ore.
Australia's iron ore exports are forecast to be A$107 billion next year, a 10% fall in value.
In an export forecast last month, Australia's industry ministry said CMRG's increasing influence "could represent a shift in market structure" with implications for iron ore price negotiations.
Miners BHP and Rio Tinto recently struck deals with CMRG, however Fortescue told investors last month its sales were 3.9 million tonnes lower because of continuing negotiations with CMRG.
If those talks are not concluded by December, the miner's operations may be impacted, Fortescue said.
432f025c9a36a30a: SAN FRANCISCO, Nov 16 — US Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent called on Nvidia to explain whether it knowingly allowed its most advanced AI chips to reach China yesterday, saying this was more important than ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with an alleged spy for Beijing.

Speaking on Fox News Sunday Morning Futures three days after Huang resigned, Bessent said he wants to know if Nvidia used shell companies to dodge US restrictions and sell its most powerful chips to China.

But late yesterday, tech tycoon Elon Musk and several other Silicon Valley leaders added their signatures to more than 165,000 others on an open letter demanding that the company’s board members “bring Jensen back while an independent investigation establishes the facts.”
The United States forbids sales to China of the most cutting-edge AI chips, hoping to stay ahead of the Chinese in the race to dominate artificial intelligence.

“Nothing above the H200s can be sold to the Chinese,” Bessent said.
“What’s more important here,” he said, “is to examine whether Nvidia had a culture of compliance around the US export restrictions.”
Bessent alluded to companies linked to Megaspeed, the Singapore-based data centre company that Huang’s alleged lover Alice Huang once worked for.
“And who knew? Because I mean, these shell companies were obvious. They were being investigated. And did Nvidia use them as a workaround to sell chips to the Chinese?”
Of Alice Huang, he said: “It doesn’t matter to me whether she’s a spy or not. You know, Jensen’s foibles are his foibles.”
Investigation deadline

Bessent said he wanted answers from Nvidia and its internal investigation of Jensen Huang’s behaviour within the next 10 days, and said the company needed “a dramatic shake-up,” which should include looking “outside” for its next chief.
The United States suspects Megaspeed helped Chinese firms get around US export controls by buying Nvidia chips for its data centers in Southeast Asia, then routing them to China.
The Justice Department is carrying out a criminal probe.
Nvidia late last month said it had investigated these allegations last year and refuted them.
The Financial Times has reported that four federal agencies pushed to have Megaspeed blacklisted by the Commerce Department run by Howard Lutnick, but the department did not do so.
“Many other departments were pushing for this, and Commerce had the pen,” Bessent said, repeating remarks he made Friday that suggest fissures in the Trump administration on this issue.

Jensen Huang and other Nvidia officials have agreed to testify in one session before representatives of three House of Representatives committees — Foreign Affairs, Intelligence, and a special committee focusing on China — Republican Congressman John Moolenaar, the chairman of that select committee, said yesterday on CBS. de0b8307018769b1: SAN FRANCISCO: No startup has ever grown so fast. In five years, Anthropic has become an AI giant valued at US$1 trillion, and it is now aiming for a record-breaking stock market debut, even if its original ambitions have been watered down somewhat.
The San Francisco-based firm faces three threats: rivals that are catching up, prices that are collapsing, and bills that keep climbing.
Anthropic spelled out the risks in its Wall Street prospectus, the document that lays out its vision to potential investors.
The first is commoditisation: "the degree of differentiation among advanced AI models may narrow," the company warns.
Additionally, Anthropic says that "substantially all" of its revenue comes from its AI tools.
Unlike Google or Meta, it has no advertising empire to fall back on if business takes a hit, and no cloud business like Microsoft's.
Investors have already grown nervous.

In mid-August, shareholders were floating a valuation of US$2 trillion. However, quarter-on-quarter growth slowed from 145% in the second quarter to 45% in the third, cooling expectations to around US$1.3 trillion.
Cheap and open
So-called open AI models, which anyone can download and modify, are approaching the capabilities of closed models such as Claude or ChatGPT, which are available only through their owners' services.
Open models lag their closed counterparts by only about four months on average, according to research institute Epoch AI.
They include Kimi K3.1 Pro from Chinese company Moonshot, which costs half as much as Claude Opus 5.5, Anthropic’s current flagship.
And among paid models from Anthropic, OpenAI and Google, none has stayed on top for long.
Anthropic also acknowledges it is holding itself back: its safety measures "could slow our capability gains relative to competitors that do not adopt similar constraints."
Still, the company says each new version of Claude has boosted sales. More than 80% of its revenue last quarter came from models less than six months old.
Prices collapsing

When products look alike, prices fall. According to Morningstar, the price of having AI process the same amount of text at the same level of performance has dropped 97%, from US$17 at the end of 2024 to 50 cents today.
Anthropic itself cut the price of Claude Opus by 20% in September, and OpenAI cut the price of one of its flagship models by a factor of five in July.
The effect is already visible at Vercel, a developer platform that routes requests across AI models.
In August, more than half of the text it handled was processed by open models, up from 13% in April.
Even so, Anthropic still captured nearly two-thirds of spending on the platform.
"Even a 90% price cut would not shrink total spending on AI as long as usage keeps growing at its current pace," said Malik Ahmed Khan, a senior equity analyst at Morningstar.
'Triple whammy'
Anthropic's costs, by contrast, are largely locked in. To stay ahead, each new Claude model has to be bigger than the last, trained on more data using more computing power.
Since late 2025, the company has committed to paying at least US$417 billion to rent chips and servers.
That is nearly 13 years of sales at its first-half 2026 pace, and the total could nearly double if cancelable or planned contracts are included.
These commitments are due no matter the state of its business, Anthropic warns.
The bet involves the entire industry: Google and Amazon are at once Anthropic's shareholders, its suppliers and its resellers.

If AI turns out to be less profitable than expected, the International Monetary Fund fears a "triple whammy" from these intertwined investments: falling stock prices, debts that are harder to repay, and promised revenue that never materializes.
The independent research firm New Constructs called the listing "an unprecedented test of investor gullibility."
To pay these bills, Anthropic is counting on money from the stock market, which is not unlimited.
SpaceX, Elon Musk's rocket and AI company, raised record sums there in June, while Google and Meta, which are pouring fortunes into data centers, are also seeking fresh capital.
OpenAI, whose chief Sam Altman called a listing "ill-advised" this year, has chosen to wait until 2027, giving it time to see how Wall Street treats its big rival.

3065e67430512f15: Amazon’s ambition to operate a constellation of broadband satellites took a hit on Sunday, when 40 of its craft failed to make it into orbit.

The failure is significant because it was the first Amazon launch to use a rocket designed especially for the job of carrying its broadband birds to low Earth orbit. The Lockheed/Boeing joint venture United Launch Alliance (ULA) created that rocket, a version of its Vulcan heavy lifter using a six-booster configuration and a Centaur V upper stage optimized to carry payloads into low Earth orbit.
Last week, Amazon previewed the launch with a post that noted this mission, code-named LV-01, is the first of 38 planned missions with ULA, and that LV-02 would likely follow within weeks.

The two companies planned to test new hardware on the first “several” flights using the custom rocket. Amazon put 40 satellites aboard the Sunday mission and said it is “already planning larger configurations for subsequent missions.”
Those plans, and the LV-02 launch, are probably on hold after the rocket suffered an anomaly 10 minutes into the flight.
The flight began well, with the Vulcan reaching an altitude of 95 miles (150 km) and completing the first phase of its flight.
Six minutes into the mission, the main booster and payload fairing both separated as planned, and ULA lit up the Centaur V’s engines for the first planned firings needed to reach low Earth orbit.
Then came the anomaly, which UAL’s live update stream states meant the mission “failed to deliver the Amazon mission to orbit.”
“Every flight generates data, and every flight teaches us something,” UAL wrote. “Since the anomaly just occurred, we don’t have any specific data yet to understand what occurred today.”
Amazon already has over 200 satellites in orbit, had hoped to launch its satellite broadband service this year, and plans 20 or more launches in 2027.
It is unclear if this mission failure will change those ambitions. ®
d2ec6581b65c222b: International executives will gather in Kuala Lumpur on Nov 16-17 to discuss cruise opportunities in Malaysia and Southeast Asia. For Malaysia, this is a significant development.
It is the first time the event is being hosted here, reflecting the growing recognition of Malaysia's considerable potential to have a more important role in the regional cruise tourism industry.

The event, Seatrade Cruise Asia 2026, brings together more than 18 international cruise line brands, including some of the biggest names such as Royal Caribbean International, StarDream Cruises, Norwegian Cruise Line, MSC Cruises, Azamara, Disney Cruise Line and Princess Cruises.

Senior executives and industry representatives from Europe, the US and Asia will participate in discussions on the future of cruising in this region, including new itineraries, emerging destinations, home-porting opportunities, port infrastructure and the growing demand for cruise holidays among Asian travellers.

Indeed, the event is being organised across several Malaysian destinations, with Kuala Lumpur hosting the main conference, followed by activities in Penang and Langkawi. This provides an opportunity to showcase not just our ports but also the country's wider tourism attractions.
Malaysia's opportunity

For many years, Singapore has established itself as the principal cruise home port in Southeast Asia. Its strategic location, international airport connectivity, modern cruise terminals and well-developed tourism infrastructure have made it a natural starting point for many international cruise operators.
From Singapore, cruise itineraries frequently extend along the Straits of Malacca, with calls at Melaka, Port Klang, Penang and Langkawi before continuing towards Phuket in Thailand.

Another attractive itinerary, depending on the season and weather conditions, covers the eastern side of the peninsula, with destinations such as Tioman, Redang and neighbouring destinations including Koh Samui in Thailand. Further itineraries can extend towards Cambodia and Vietnam, which includes Sihanoukville, Ho Chi Minh City and Da Nang.

All these routes offer considerable opportunities for Malaysia. We have the geographical advantage of being located along some of the busiest and most established maritime tourism corridors in Southeast Asia.
We also have a diverse range of destinations, from historical cities and cultural attractions to islands, beaches, rainforests and natural landscapes.

However, geographical location alone does not guarantee success. Cruise operators are commercial businesses. They look at passenger demand, port accessibility, terminal facilities, operating costs, immigration procedures, shore excursions and the overall attractiveness of destinations before deciding where to deploy their vessels.
Growing Asian market
The timing is particularly important because the Asian cruise market is developing rapidly.

According to figures released by the Singapore Tourism Board, Southeast Asia recorded approximately 3.9 million cruise passenger visits in 2024. Singapore accounted for 48% of these visits, while Malaysia captured approximately 22%.
Together, the two countries accounted for around 70% of the growing regional market. These figures also demonstrate that Malaysia is already an important cruise destination.

However, it has also been suggested that there is considerable room to grow, particularly if we can attract more international cruise operators and encourage more Malaysians to experience cruise holidays.

The potential domestic market should not be underestimated either. Malaysia has a sizeable middle-income population, an expanding travelling public and a growing number of families looking for alternative holiday experiences.

Cruise holidays could become increasingly attractive, particularly for families who prefer an all-inclusive holiday package with accommodation, meals, entertainment and multiple destinations incorporated into one journey.
There is also an opportunity to develop more regional cruise packages catering specifically to Malaysian, Indonesian, Thai and other Southeast Asian travellers.
This is a growing market that cruise operators are looking to explore and I think Malaysia is ready for it.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

5a2587b6eab93678: Sabtu lalu, Menteri Besar Negeri Sembilan, Ismail Lasim, mengesahkan beliau telah menarik balik surat yang dihantar kepada Penyimpan Mohor Besar Raja-raja berhubung 'penyingkiran' Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan.
Surat itu juga difahamkan mengesahkan sokongan sebulat suara bekas 10 anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri terhadap Tuanku Muhriz.

Ini membawa kita kepada soalan satu juta ringgit: Bolehkah kita meletakkan kepercayaan kepada Umno Negeri Sembilan? Adakah kata-kata mereka benar-benar ikhlas? Atau adakah ini satu lagi helah untuk cuba menjatuhkan pemerintah negeri?
Teguran terbuka Tuanku Muhriz terhadap Ismail baru-baru ini secara tidak langsung menggambarkan Ismail sebagai seorang yang tidak boleh dipercayai.
Terdapat empat sebab mengapa saya masih sangsi terhadap tindakan Ismail.

1. Kenapa baru sekarang Ismail menarik balik surat itu? Teori saya ialah beliau memerlukan perkenan untuk mengadakan sidang DUN. Walaupun dari segi teori menteri besar boleh mentadbir sesebuah negeri tanpa anggota Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri, sidang DUN diperlukan untuk meluluskan belanjawan dan rang undang-undang.
Perkara ini menimbulkan persoalan: adakah Ismail benar-benar insaf atas tindakannya? Atau beliau hanya terdesak?
2. Tindakan Ismail ketika kontroversi itu

Tindakan Ismail menggambarkan dengan jelas mengenai beliau. Sebelum ini, Ismail berkata beliau dipaksa menandatangani dokumen untuk menurunkan Tuanku Muhriz, namun kemudian menyokong kenyataan Majlis Mesyuarat Kerajaan Negeri yang mengumumkan pemerintah negeri itu telah diturunkan.

Pada 2 Ogos, Ismail mengangkat sumpah sebagai menteri besar di hadapan Tuanku Muhriz dan melafazkan ikrar taat setia kepada baginda. Sehari selepas itu, Ismail menandatangani pengisytiharan untuk menurunkan pemerintah negeri itu.
Ada pepatah yang berbunyi, 'sekali terkena, dua kali beringat'. Namun, dalam keadaan ini, kita sepatutnya empat kali beringat.
3. Isu Undang Luak yang masih belum selesai
Masih terdapat isu membabitkan Undang Luak, termasuk beberapa orang yang telah diturunkan, serta individu yang dilantik oleh mereka sebagai Yang Dipertuan Besar yang baharu.

Kumpulan ini masih rancak dengan aktiviti mereka, dilihat tidak menunjukkan sebarang kekesalan atas tindakan mereka apabila secara terbuka mencabar notis warta Dewan Keadilan dan Undang (DKU) yang mengesahkan penyingkiran dua Undang dan seorang pemimpin adat.
Dikatakan kumpulan ini mempunyai hubungan rapat dengan Adun Umno Negeri Sembilan. Perlu diingat, tiada seorang pun Adun Umno tampil secara terbuka menolak kumpulan tersebut.
Jadi, bagaimana kita sebagai rakyat boleh menaruh kepercayaan terhadap tindakan Ismail menarik balik surat itu sedangkan Umno dipercayai masih mempunyai kaitan dengan kumpulan berkenaan?

4. Adakah Ismail memberikan jaminan melalui perisytiharan bertulis yang ditandatangani bahawa beliau dan kumpulan anggota Umnonya tidak akan sekali-kali lagi berpakat dengan pihak lain untuk menjatuhkan Tuanku Muhriz? Jika Ismail benar-benar insaf, beliau sepatutnya menunjukkan lebih untuk membuktikannya.

Kini, kemenangan besar Umno dalam PRN Melaka akan memberikan parti itu sedikit kelebihan untuk berbangga susulan kontroversi isu tahanan rumah bekas perdana menteri Najib Razak serta kewangan Felda dan Lembaga Tabung Haji, yang tidak menjejaskan sokongan terhadap parti itu.

Tak banyak sebab untuk saya mempercayai Ismail dan Umno Negeri Sembilan ini benar-benar insaf dengan kesalahan mereka.

a8becbed55c716fd: On Saturday, Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Ismail Lasim confirmed he had withdrawn a letter sent to the Keeper of the Rulers’ Seal concerning the “removal” of Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir as the Yang Dipertuan Besar of Negeri Sembilan.
The letter was also understood to affirm the unanimous support of the 10 sacked executive council members for Tuanku Muhriz.

This brings us to the million-ringgit question: can we trust Negeri Sembilan Umno? Is there any sincerity in what they say? Or is this yet another sleight of hand in an attempt to topple the state ruler?
Tuanku Muhriz's recent public rebuke of Ismail does not paint the latter as someone trustworthy.
There are four reasons why I remain wary of Ismail’s actions.

1. Why is Ismail retracting the letter only now? My theory is that he needs the ruler’s consent to convene the state assembly. While one could, on paper, administer a state without executive councillors, a state assembly sitting is needed to pass budgets and proposed laws.
Which raises this question: is Ismail really remorseful for his actions? Or is he acting out of desperation?
2. Ismail’s actions amid the controversy

They speak volumes about the man himself. He previously said he was coerced into signing a document deposing Tuanku Muhriz, only to later endorse a state executive council statement announcing the ruler’s purported removal.
On Aug 2, Ismail took his oath of office as menteri besar and pledged allegiance to Tuanku Muhriz before signing a proclamation the following day to remove the ruler.
There is a saying, “once bitten, twice shy”. In this instance though, we should be shy four times over.
3. There is still the matter of the other undangs (traditional territorial chieftains), some of whom have been removed, and the matter of the person whom they appointed as the state’s new ruler.

This faction, which is still alive and kicking, has apparently shown no remorse for its actions by openly challenging a Dewan Keadilan dan Undang Negeri Sembilan gazette notice formalising the removal of two chieftains and a customary leader.
It is said that this faction is close to Umno assemblymen in Negeri Sembilan. Mind you, none of the Umno assemblymen have come out to publicly distance themselves from this faction.
So how can we, the people, have any faith in Ismail’s retraction of a letter when Umno is presumably still linked to the said faction?

4. Has Ismail provided assurance via a written and signed declaration that he and his band of Umno men will never again conspire with others to overthrow Tuanku Muhriz? If Ismail were truly repentant, he would have gone the extra mile to show it.

Now, Umno’s decisive win at the Melaka polls will give the party some bragging rights following the controversies over former prime minister Najib Razak’s house arrest and the finances of Felda or Tabung Haji, which did not dent support for the party.
A resurgent Umno is likely to be emboldened to pull off another stunt in Negeri Sembilan, seeing as how the first one didn’t pan out exactly as they planned.
Ismail Lasim and Negeri Sembilan Umno give me very little reason to trust this mea culpa.

13c955d113761972: It began, as most modern Malaysian sagas do, not with a bang, but with a grumble. A mamak shop, that near-sacred 24-hour temple of roti canai and teh tarik, had the audacity to close its doors on Deepavali day.

The reason? To allow its staff, many of whom are Hindus, to celebrate the Festival of Lights. A simple, humane and frankly logical decision. And yet, within hours, it had ignited a firestorm on social media, transforming a shop’s holiday schedule into a national debate on race, religion and the soul of our nation.
This can only happen in Malaysia. “Mamak tutup? On Deepavali? How can a Muslim-run restaurant close for a Hindu-based celebration?” So began the stream of religious insults and slurs.

For most people, the mamak shop is more than a restaurant; it is a cultural institution, a neutral ground where everyone can sit side-by-side at 3am, arguing over football or who should be the prime minister.

But the debate triggered by the post made out the closure to be almost a betrayal of the social contract. The real fireworks began when the keyboard warriors logged on and the debate fractured along predictable, yet deeply depressing, lines.

On one side, some who described the closure as an act of placing Deepavali celebrations over Islam, an analogy that is mind-boggling. On the other side, those who celebrated the closure as a victory for inclusivity, while simultaneously weaponising it against the owners. A simple act of employee appreciation became a truncheon in the never-ending racial culture war.

The comments sections devolved into a cesspool of racial slurs and religious mockery. The practices of each community – from fasting to praying to celebrating – were dissected, mocked and used as ammunition.

This is the Malaysian paradox. We are a nation that prides itself on our diversity, our muhibbah spirit and our ability to live together. We celebrate each other's festivals with open houses and open hearts. But the moment a minor racial or religious issue is raised, the harmony ruptures and the nation's ugly, tribalistic underbelly is exposed for all to see.

The debate exposed a deep-seated insecurity, the fear of being marginalised, anxiety over the “other” and the constant, exhausting need to assert one's own identity in a multi-racial landscape. The mamak shop became a proxy for a much larger, unresolved national conversation about what it means to be Malaysian.

The fact that we lose our minds over such a small matter is precisely the problem. We have become experts at finding offence, at drawing battle lines over the most trivial of issues. A shop closure becomes a religious war. A wrong word becomes a racial slur. A difference in opinion becomes a declaration of enmity.
We are so quick to insult each other, yet so slow to extend the basic courtesy of understanding.

The next time you see a shop closed for a holiday that isn't “yours”, take a breath. Instead of reaching for your phone to type a scathing comment, maybe reach for a packet of murukku from a Hindu neighbour.
The mamak shop will reopen, but the damage done by our own intolerance, the scars we inflict on our national psyche with every hateful comment, are far harder to heal.
Only in Malaysia can a day of light be turned into a war of darkness. Sadly, that is the most Malaysian thing of all.
The views expressed are those of the writer and do not necessarily reflect those of FMT.

90f0751c0696ac91: Microsoft has announced massive price rises for commercial cloud services in India and New Zealand, but a substantial reduction in China.
The software giant sells its cloudy services in many local currencies, at an equivalent rate to the prices it charges in the USA.

Australian buyers will see costs fall by 4.5 percent. The only nation not in Asia on Microsoft’s list is Norway, where prices will ease 5.9 percent.

Sega has just had a rotten week that saw it battle a data leak and an outage.

Alibaba floats chip unit
Chinese tech giant Alibaba last week announced its intention to float its T-Head chip design biz on the Hong Kong Stock Exchange.

The filing announcing the spinoff describes T-Head as “a leading provider of full-stack data center chips which enable system-level compute solutions in China,” suggesting Alibaba doesn’t think buyers in the rest of the world are keen to acquire its chips.

T-Head going public “allows a more efficient deployment of Alibaba Group’s financial resources,” the filing states, and should also mean the chip design outfit can more easily find third-party customers.
India bans export of dead batteries
The government of India last week banned the export of “Lithium-Ion battery Black Mass” – a powdery substance created during the process of recycling batteries.

“It contains recoverable quantities of critical minerals, including lithium, cobalt, nickel and manganese,” according to the government’s announcement of the ban, which argues the measure “will increase domestic recovery of lithium, cobalt, nickel and other critical minerals, thereby reducing import dependence and the associated foreign exchange outgo. It will also strengthen supply chains for battery manufacturing, electric vehicles, energy storage and clean-energy technologies.”

“Further, the measure will advance the circular economy and ‘urban mining’, reducing reliance on primary mining, while supporting environmentally sound recycling of this hazardous material within the country in accordance with applicable environmental regulations.”
Japanese giants to investigate orbiting datacenters

Five giant Japanese companies – NTT, Mitsubishi Electric, MUFG Bank, the Development Bank of Japan, and telco NTT DOCOMO – last week signed a memorandum of understanding that will see them jointly explore development and operation of a mega-constellation of satellites.

The five “will examine the technical and business feasibility of commercializing a diverse range of services enabled by mega-constellations, including communications, Earth observation, satellite-based positioning, navigation, and timing (PNT), and space data centers.”

Mitsubishi already works with the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) to jointly develop and manufacture rockets. The two banks regularly back big infrastructure projects, while the two NTT entities have advanced comms expertise.
The five companies didn’t set a deadline for delivery of a plan.

If they do decide there’s a business opportunity, they’ll likely need to look beyond Japan for launch capacity as JAXA does not currently possess a re-usable launch vehicle and operates at a modest launch cadence compared to private launch operators. ®

4e3b3836efc8ff88: From Hisham Aziz

The corporate anxieties following the tabling of Budget 2027 prompt a critical question: when did Malaysia’s apex industry associations transform from champions of free-market resilience into professional victims of helplessness?
The press releases and policy papers issued by the Federation of Malaysian Manufacturers (FMM) suffer from structural issues that expose their lack of analytical weight and credibility.

FMM’s press statements exhibit the distinct characteristics of automated text generation — relying heavily on template-driven headers, passive phrasing, and generic buzzword aggregation like “supply chain resilience” and “digital transformation” in place of plant-level operational data. This reliance on high-level abstraction obscures true empirical rigor.

Rather than presenting detailed microeconomic data, unit-cost offsets, or lead-time data, FMM’s advocacy frequently uses sweeping language backed by disproportionately small survey sample sizes to demand massive policy concessions like credit lines, grant facilities, and tax deferments.
To the public and policymakers, organisations like FMM present themselves as fragile, over-burdened entities teetering on the edge of ruin due to basic regulatory adjustments.

Yet, a glance at public policy performance reveals an entirely different reality. These bodies represent the primary beneficiaries of decades of state largesse — enjoying extensive energy subsidies, infrastructure support, and generous tax incentives.

Under Budget 2027, this patronage continues unabated with fresh financing facilities from Bank Negara Malaysia (BNM) alongside a transitional exemption from the RM2,000 minimum wage threshold for micro, small, and medium enterprises (MSMEs).
Despite this comprehensive safety net, the lobbying apparatus remains ever unquenchable.

In October 2026, FMM publicly expressed deep disappointment, lamenting a “lack of support” for the manufacturing sector simply because the government did not grant their requested RM1.5 billion extra support package. The danger lies not just in this sense of entitlement, but in the dubious, lightweight methodologies used to justify it.

Consider the statistical acrobatics deployed to influence national economic policy. In June 2026, FMM issued sweeping, alarmist warnings about global supply chain shocks — specifically the impact of the Strait of Hormuz conflict on domestic oil prices and SME survival.
The data to back these massive macroeconomic warnings? A survey pool of exactly 196 companies (FMM Geopolitical Impact Survey, June 2026).
To suggest that a survey pool smaller than a single mid-size factory floor can accurately reflect the structural vulnerabilities of Malaysia’s entire SME sector is absurd.
Yet, it is precisely on the back of these minuscule data sets that case studies are built to demand more credit lines, heavier grants, and broad credit deferments from the taxpayer.

This audacity reaches its peak when looking at their tax advocacy. In their September 2026 Business Conditions Survey (1H2026) briefing, FMM aggressively pushed for a return to the Goods and Services Tax (GST) but demanded it be implemented at a rock-bottom introductory rate of 3.0% — down from the historic 6% floor.
According to FMM’s own polling, while 68% of respondents demanded a rate below 5%, a full 41% explicitly called for a 3% rate.

How peak industrial representatives can genuinely look at Malaysia’s expanding national expenditure and rising infrastructure commitments and suggest halving consumption tax revenues is a great wonder.
They demand that public tax collection be gutted for their operational convenience, while simultaneously expecting the public purse to keep funding their multi-billion-ringgit economic safety nets.
FMM’s platform runs completely counter to the Madani government’s explicit agenda to transition Malaysia away from its unhealthy dependency on low-cost, low-skilled migrant labour.
By fighting tooth and nail against statutory wage floors and basic family protections, FMM is actively working to keep Malaysian wages artificially suppressed.
This short-sighted resistance eliminates the exact economic pressure businesses need to innovate.

If labour is kept artificially cheap through state exemptions and structural suppression, manufacturing firms will feel zero urgency to invest in research and development (R&D), upgrade their technology, or pursue genuine, automation-led productivity growth.
It is not possible to build an Industry 4.0 economy on an automated AI-generated script that begs to preserve an Industry 2.0 labour pool.
This irony peaks when looking at how FMM constructs its internal narratives.
In that same 1H2026 Survey, FMM dedicated an entire section to aggressively policing government administration, using curated survey questions to put HRD Corp in a distinctly negative light.

FMM explicitly complained that HRD Corp’s revised e-TRiS grant conditions actively “hindered training and planning” for 44% of businesses, highlighting that rigid bureaucratic rules — like the mandatory 14-day advance approval window — made it nearly impossible to provide urgent training.

FMM will meticulously poll its members to complain about public sector administrative flexibility, and they will rightfully demand accountability following HRD Corp’s financial mismanagement scandals.

Yet, they weaponize these administrative hurdles as a convenient shield to demand that training funds remain entirely under corporate autonomy. We see this exact transactional morality in their response to parental benefits.

While FMM aggressively fought the statutory 98-day maternity leave mandate as an unbearable operational cost when forced to pay for it, they happily celebrate the newly proposed Budget 2027 post-maternity allowance simply because the state is funding it through the Employment Insurance System (EIS).

They expect national tax revenues to be minimised and public funding maximised whenever it protects their corporate ledger but completely reject socioeconomic flexibility when asked to internally finance a liveable wage or grant a recovering mother an extra month of leave.
The government must stop treating these large corporate blocks as fragile patients in need of permanent economic life support.
True economic restructuring requires rigorous data, authentic feedback, and shared sacrifice. Not fake narratives and political manipulation.
Policymakers should look past the AI-generated statements and reports based on questionable methodologies and unreliable sample sizes and look closely at the empirical reality.

Malaysia’s industrial sector is well-capitalised and heavily subsidised. It is time they scaled up through innovation, automation, and R&D, rather than lobbying their way out of basic social contracts.
Malaysia’s manufacturing cannot be on permanent life-support to pander to a small group of people, nor held ransom by people using trade associations for their political agenda.
Hisham Aziz is an FMT reader.

10dd1d36af4191ae: DHAKA, Nov 16 — Unions representing Bangladeshi garment manufacturers threatened on
Saturday to walk away from wage negotiations and shut factories indefinitely if protesters kept vandalising them during demonstrations for higher pay.

Bangladesh is the world’s second-largest garment exporter after China, producing clothes for major international brands like Fruit of the Loom, Levi Strauss and VF Corp, whose labels include Vans, Timberland and The North Face.
Worker unrest over wages began in October and has occasionally turned violent, with demonstrators torching police vehicles and damaging property during clashes this month.

The two main manufacturing unions – the Bangladesh Garment Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BGMEA) and the Bangladesh Knitwear Manufacturers and Exporters Association (BKMEA) – sharpened their rhetoric on Saturday.

“BGMEA and BKMEA have questioned the justification of continuing to participate in wage board negotiations without any assurance that the factories will be protected,” BGMEA President Mahmud Hasan Khan said at a news briefing in the capital Dhaka.
“If the situation persists, we must reconsider,” Khan said.
“Garment factories that have been unable to continue production due to the ongoing unrest will remain indefinitely closed from tomorrow under... Bangladesh’s labour law,” he added.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Garment workers rally in Dhaka on November 13, 2026 demanding a US$260 (RM982) minimum wage. — NurPhoto pic via AFP
The “no work, no pay” provision of Bangladesh labour law allows factory owners to suspend operations without paying workers.
Workers say rising food, housing, transport and healthcare costs have eroded their purchasing power in a country where inflation is running at around eight per cent.
Shutdown notices
They are demanding a minimum monthly wage of 30,000 taka (US$240; RM982) — a 140-per cent increase on the current 12,500 taka (RM409).

The protests have threatened to disrupt an industry that earns around US$38 billion (RM155.4 billion) annually, accounting for four-fifths of Bangladesh’s export earnings and employing more than four million workers.
Some 147 factories remained closed on Saturday in Savar, Ashulia and Gazipur – the country’s main garment manufacturing hubs.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Security guards keep watch at the gate of a closed textile factory in Dhaka on November 14, 2026, amid garment workers’ protests for higher pay. — AFP pic
More than 4,500 factories are registered with trade bodies like the BGMEA.
Workers staged fresh demonstrations in Gazipur on Saturday, blocking traffic for more than an hour before they were dispersed by law enforcement officers.
Managers at some of the dozens of closed factories in Ashulia posted notices announcing indefinite shutdowns.
Mazharul Islam, general manager of S-21 Apparels Limited, said a group of workers had disrupted operations despite most employees reporting for duty.
<!--article_body_images.blade.php-->
Bangladesh border guards patrol a street outside a textile factory in Dhaka on November 14, 2026, amid garment workers’ protests for higher pay. — AFP pic
“Around 95 per cent of workers came to work as usual on Thursday morning, while a few angry workers started shouting and forcing others to leave the factory,” he said.
“They vandalised the facility, and we had to announce its closure to protect the factory.”
The disruption comes during the run-up to Christmas, the busiest export period for Bangladesh’s garment industry.
“Due to the war (in Middle East), it takes an additional 10 days for shipments to reach their destinations, and now with this unrest... the sector is surely under threat,” Islam said.
Security has been tightened across industrial zones, with Border Guard Bangladesh and police personnel patrolling areas near factories. — AFP
