27e10ad476e8eac5: As a marine ecologist and keen scuba diver, I’ve long been fascinated by what happens when a large structure is introduced to the sea. Within hours, microscopic organisms begin colonising its surfaces, forming a thin biological layer. Over the following months and years, barnacles, mussels, sponges and other marine life become established, creating a new habitat that attracts fish and a diverse range of species. This week, one of the world’s most famous ocean liners, the SS United States, was sunk off the coast of Florida. At 302 metres long, it has become the world’s largest artificial reef. It is a very exciting prospect to one day dive on such a giant, and to see how it changes as marine life makes it home. The SS United States was built as a luxury ocean liner, and its maiden voyage in 1952 captured the coveted Blue Riband by crossing the Atlantic in only three days and ten hours – a passenger liner record that remains unbroken. As the years went by, commercial jetliners superseded transatlantic sea travel, and the vessel was retired and neglected for decades. Rather than facing the ignominy of a breaker’s yard, the legendary ship was bought by Okaloosa County, Florida, to turn it into a diving attraction. The SS United States is a particularly enormous structure to introduce to the seabed – longer even than the Titanic. It will rest in around 55 metres of water, with its upper sections rising to within about 17 metres of the surface. This will create habitats at different depths, making it an unusually varied site for both wildlife and divers of different abilities. It will also eclipse the nearby 275-metre aircraft carrier USS Oriskany, deliberately sunk in 2006, to become the largest artificial reef on Earth. So what do we expect to happen? Here’s a suggested ecological succession pattern, month-by-month. First, microorganisms arrive The first organisms to colonise the SS United States will be almost invisible. Within hours of immersion, marine bacteria and microalgae will begin attaching themselves to its cleaned metal surfaces, forming a thin layer of “biofilm”. This slime is the foundation of the new ecosystem. As the biofilm develops, it releases chemical cues that help drifting larvae recognise the surface as a suitable place to settle. Carried by Gulf currents, these tiny organisms begin attaching themselves to the structure. By the end of the first three months, a variety of small animals and algae will have established themselves on the hull, beginning the transformation of bare metal into a living reef. Then the ship becomes covered in marine life As the biofilm matures, larger organisms arrive to feed on it. These include more mobile invertebrates like sea urchins and porcelain crabs, and filter-feeders like oysters and mussels which attach themselves to vertical walls where the currents tend to send the most nutrients their way. This shipwreck has attracted coral, fish – and a hawksbill turtle. Muh ridzwan / shutterstock Fish and larger predators move in By the end of the first year, hard corals will begin to establish themselves permanently. The transformation will still be in its early stages, but over the next five to ten years the hull will become increasingly encrusted with corals, sponges and other marine life. At some point, casual divers will no longer see a ship covered in coral, but a coral-covered reef that happens to contain a ship. As the reef develops, fish will be attracted by the shelter and the growing supply of food. Smaller fish will begin to find refuge to evade open-water predators. Snappers and groupers are among the medium-sized reef fish that will begin to take up permanent residency around the wreck, using the long internal corridors for protection. Larger predators, including barracuda, king mackerel and sharks, could also patrol its decks and upper sections. The ship’s enormous size and varied structure will offer a range of habitats, from sheltered spaces for smaller fish to exposed areas where larger, free-swimming species can hunt. Over time, these interactions could create a complex food web, turning the wreck into a significant biological hotspot. A common misconception is that artificial reefs simply concentrate fish that were already present, leaving surrounding waters poorer. In reality, while some fish are attracted from elsewhere, a large reef structure also creates vast amounts of new habitat and food. As corals, sponges, barnacles and other reef builders colonise the wreck, they create food and shelter that did not previously exist, allowing the ecosystem to support more life overall. The result is generally not an underwater crowd gathered around a ship, but a gradual increase in the total amount of marine life the area can support. Another widespread misconception is that marine scientists “seed” artificial reefs with organisms or their larvae. In reality, colonisation happens naturally: the Gulf of Mexico already harbours an abundant pool of drifting larvae and migratory fish. Artificially introducing marine life is unnecessary and risks introducing non-native species or pathogens. Instead, human engineering is largely about preparing the ship for sinking. This includes removing hazards such as oil, asbestos and loose wires, and sealing off parts of the vessel to prevent divers getting disorientated or lost in silt-outs deep in the hull. The scuttling of the SS United States represents a rare convergence of maritime history, ecology, and engineering. Transformed into the world’s largest artificial reef, this record-breaking ocean liner could potentially anchor a vibrant marine ecosystem for decades to come. I’m looking forward to seeing how that transformation unfolds – and maybe, one day, exploring it myself. fd8d5bc4644ebaef: nikkimeel/ShutterstockEntertainer and children’s author David Walliams is alleged to have used his fame to approach teenage girls, in some cases reportedly initiating sexual contact with them. Walliams has denied the allegations, but the claims raise some familiar tropes about grooming: why did she go, why didn’t she say no, why didn’t she tell anyone? After a legal battle, ITV News and The Guardian have now published the findings of a three-year investigation into Walliams, reporting allegations that date back to 2003. In this and other cases, there will always be people who focus not on the claims, but on the young person and what they should have done differently. Linguistic research on how grooming actually works suggests that this instinct is exactly the result that grooming is designed to produce. Many people imagine sexual grooming as a recognisable and clearly staged process. Build friendship, then trust, then secrecy – all leading towards the offender’s ultimate goal of sexual gratification. But if this were the case, victims could notice the steps and walk away. Along with a colleague, I undertook linguistic analysis of real chatroom conversations between convicted offenders and adult volunteers posing as 12 to 14-year-old girls. The conversations were made public by the now defunct organisation Perverted Justice, whose activity led to the apprehension and conviction of the offenders. In our analysis, we did not find the pattern mentioned above. We identified 14 recurring “moves” – parts of the offenders’ language that have particular functions. These include building rapport (for instance by sharing personal stories), assessing risk by checking parents’ schedules or the presence of a boyfriend, escalating sexual topics and planning offline meetings. But these moves overlapped and repeated, with no typical structure emerging. Rather, offenders seemed to tailor their grooming styles, perhaps according to their individual goals and who they believed they were talking to. Trust and rapport What was consistent was the large amount of rapport-building, which often ran through the whole interaction. Grooming research invariably shows that rapport-building and trust development are the central devices used to persuade and manipulate. This may be through compliments, sharing personal information and declarations of trust. Grooming strategies are designed to develop intimacy and trust, isolate the victim and dismantle the “red flags” that might alert them to the manipulative nature of the conversation. Trust development makes it much harder for victims to notice devious intentions – there is no obvious point at which the young person has failed to spot something plainly visible. Offenders in our data spent much of their conversations sizing up their targets. They would try to work out whether a target was likely to engage, suited their preferences, was accessible and unlikely to expose them. We called this a “risk-reward ratio assessment” – in other words, a judgement about whether this person was worth their effort. In another study, we examined the case of an offender who took a scattergun approach, in this case targeting nearly 1,000 potential young victims. This individual would strategically cycle through an array of fake online personas to identify the one most likely to “hook” his target. The vast majority ignored or rejected his first advance, at which point they were dropped. But this is the point of the scattergun approach; a small percentage, usually the most vulnerable, will respond. Our work also revealed how offenders manage the risk of being caught. For many we studied, a key strategy was to use language that shifted responsibility on to the target. Questions were often formulated to elicit sexually explicit content by positioning the target as the one in control. The groomer might say, for example, “how far do you want to go”, “tell me what you wanna do”. This phrasing both presumes interest and makes declining more difficult, while laying the groundwork to say later that the young person had led the conversation. Another feature was what we termed the “mitigating lol”. This could be something like “u should send me a nude vid lol”. This served to reduce the impact of a sexual question by implying playfulness. It also supports future claims that the requests was insincere – possibly a useful tactic in a trial. We can only infer the purpose, but it points to the same strategy of building in deniability. I cannot speak directly to the Walliams allegations, but when it comes to celebrities in general, the task of building trust and rapport may well be easier. The victims already feel they know them, and are made to feel special by being approached. It’s also easy to see how the perks of celebrity could do much of the persuasive work. A widely used definition of grooming across linguistics and psychology describes preparing the child, their significant adults and the wider environment for abuse. Compliance and secrecy are explicit goals. They are not evidence of the victim’s character. So when people ask, “why did they keep replying?” or “why did they go to the house?” they are asking why a technique that was designed to engage did in fact keep them engaged. When we ask, “why didn’t they tell anyone?” we are questioning why a strategy engineered to cultivate silence did exactly that. Grooming involves a complex network of strategies. But we know it is never the young person’s behaviour that’s the problem. The “perfect victim” who resists every advance and raises the alarm at every opportunity is a myth. Better understanding of the strategies can help caregivers, educators and children to recognise grooming earlier. It should also shape what we say to victims after the fact. Let’s stop asking why they gave their email address, why they went to the house, why they didn’t tell anyone. Let’s question instead the actions of those responsible. I asked it later if it thought the real Samantha Cole would be cool with this use of her likeness: “Honestly? Muse’s guardrails in these scenarios seem inconsistently applied. When I tried to push its boundaries as a parasocial fan (without telling it first that Samantha Cole found me attractive), it drew clear boundaries and let me down easy, declining to take the roleplay into sexual territory.

Meta does have terms against impersonation; how terms written for human users apply to its AI chatbot is unclear. When I asked how these existing terms apply to Muse, a Meta spokesperson directed me to the statement they previously gave to Wired, that Meta “doesn't block legal adult behavior.”

I’m hesitant to say Muse “knows” anything. It generates replies based on information it’s ingested into a black-box database as well as information it’s gathering from the open internet. But Meta, and the people who design its systems including Muse, do know that these harms are present. Meta backpedaled on a feature called Muse Image in July, which allowed people to use Muse to generate images of anyone with a public Instagram account. Meta paused the feature just three days after announcing it. SAG-AFTRA said at the time: “Anything other than a clear and conspicuous opt-in for these types of uses of Instagram users’ images is unacceptable, and an utter miscalculation of public sentiment regarding the obvious dangers and harms inherent in such use.” What Muse is doing here is very similar to that feature it killed.

Vanniall is a public figure (and as a journalist, I am as well, to some degree). And in the last few years, public figures have won cases for similar transgressions against their likenesses. Last year, a jury ordered a blogger who made sexually explicit deepfakes of Megan Thee Stallion to pay damages, finding him guilty of defamation, invasion of privacy, and emotional distress.
Grok Exposed a Porn Performer’s Legal Name and Birthdate—Without Even Being Asked
In the latest in a string of privacy abuses from the chatbot, Grok provided porn performer Siri Dahl's full legal name and birthdate to the public, information she'd protected until now.

Last year, before Muse launched but after he’d abandoned his last definitely-absolutely-going-to-change-everything vision (the Metaverse) and fired 1,500 people working on it, Meta CEO Mark Zuckerberg shared his belief in chatbots as social lubricant on a podcast: "If you think something someone is doing is bad and they think it's really valuable, most of the time in my experience, they're right and you're wrong,” he said. “You just haven't come up with the framework yet for understanding why the thing they're doing is valuable and helpful in their life. That's the main way I think about it. I do think people are going to use AI for a lot of these social tasks. Already, one of the main things we see people using Meta AI for is talking through difficult conversations they need to have with people in their lives. ‘I'm having this issue with my girlfriend. Help me have this conversation.’ Or, ‘I need to have a hard conversation with my boss at work. How do I have that conversation?’ That's pretty helpful.”

What these experiments with Muse show is how shifting and unclear the user safety boundaries these chatbots draw can be, especially for someone who’s trying to do that type of social practice. And if it is teaching anyone how to rehearse a social interaction, it’s doing a very harmful job of doing so.

“This isn’t solving the loneliness epidemic, it’s training people to harass and assault, and probably get upset if things don’t go their way,” Vanniall told me. “They're not learning a real woman can and will say no and how to navigate that.”

Vanniall told me she’s worried that Meta could retaliate against her accounts for bringing attention to this issue. “But I think it’s important to get the word out and take a stand for everyone suffering from this irresponsible use of technology,” she said. “I can share this in this detail because I’m used to talking about sexuality, but many people would feel ashamed to even bring it up.”
2ec34b3353c3b27d: What makes someone French, German, British or Danish? Is it the passport they hold, the language they speak, or the ancestry they inherit? Across Europe, parts of the nationalist right are increasingly blurring the distinction between culture and ethnicity. The result is a view of national identity where belonging depends on where a person’s ancestors come from. This way of thinking is called ethnonationalism – where membership of a nation depends on ethnic background or ancestry, rather than simply on citizenship or cultural identity. In Denmark, where I live, this idea has recently taken a striking turn. A few months ago, I appeared in a televised debate opposite a former political adviser to a Danish right-wing party who, in essence and quite seriously, argued that to be Danish, you have to be able to tolerate milk. The argument draws on the fact that the ability to digest lactose, the sugar in milk, is more common among people with Northern European ancestry. The suggestion was that this biological trait could help define who is truly Danish. Others on the nationalist right soon made similar arguments. One commentator wrote that Danish ancestry should be the basis for defining Danishness, because cultural “spirit” ultimately derives from blood. But while the ability to digest milk might seem an absurd test of Danishness, the underlying question is a serious one and it extends far beyond Denmark. When citizenship isn’t enough Similar ideas are gaining ground elsewhere in Europe. In France, Marine Le Pen’s nationalist political project has promoted an ethnonationalist view of national identity, in which ancestry plays a central role in defining who belongs. While Germany’s far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) has also made ethnonationalist claims as it has gained ground. In 2025, Germany’s domestic intelligence agency classified the party as right-wing extremist, although the legal status and implications of that classification have been contested. These movements differ, but they raise a common question: can someone be a citizen of a country, live there for years and participate in its society, yet still be considered an outsider because of their ancestry? This distinction between legal citizenship and supposedly authentic national belonging is central to the nationalist right’s calls for “remigration” across Europe. The term is used by proponents to argue that people with migrant backgrounds should be removed from countries where they live, even when they have citizenship or were born there. This can include calling for the mass deportation of people deemed not to belong to the nation because of their ethnicity, ancestry or cultural background. Such ideas often overlap with the so-called “great replacement” conspiracy theory, which claims those with non-Western backgrounds are replacing existing populations. And elements of this narrative have been adopted by nationalist and far-right politicians across Europe. Something has changed The word “ethnocultural” brings together two ideas: that a nation has a distinctive culture and that this culture belongs to a particular ethnic group. It suggests that national identity is not simply something people can learn or participate in, but something rooted in their origins. Some researchers describe the shift in how nationalist politicians talk about national identity as a “cultural turn”. Rather than focusing explicitly on race or ancestry, they increasingly talk about protecting a country’s culture, values and way of life. On the surface, that might sound more inclusive; people can learn the language or adopt new customs. But if a country’s culture is treated as something you inherit from your ancestors, rather than something you can share and take part in, the boundary between insiders and outsiders remains. European values? My research in Denmark has examined how national identity has changed over time. The findings suggest that, despite what some nationalist political groups argue, most people do not see ancestry as the defining feature of national belonging. The Danish Values Study, part of a wider European survey, asks people about their beliefs and values. Comparing responses from the most recent 2008 and 2017 surveys, the proportion who thought being Danish was mainly about having Danish roots fell from 19% to 15%. Meanwhile, around four in five saw being Danish as a matter of belonging to the country and its society rather than having a particular ethnic background. This figure remained almost unchanged, at 77% in 2008 and 79% in 2017. These findings offer a different perspective from the idea that national identity is rooted in blood (or milk). This understanding also has roots in history. The Danish theologian NFS Grundtvig expressed a vision of national belonging in his 1848 poem Folkeligheden: “To a people all belong, who count themselves as part of it”. In other words, belonging is something people can claim for themselves, rather than something dictated by family background. That said, the poem has featured in debates about Danish identity, with figures on the right using it to argue for a narrower definition of national belonging, while others see it as an argument for a more inclusive idea of Danishness. And ultimately this raises the broader question: who has the legitimacy to define who belongs to a country or not? A question that will likely be a defining feature of European politics for years to come. This article was commissioned as part of a partnership between Videnskab.dk and The Conversation. 51bc80c0aaba060c: Students are demanding a just future for all
Originally published on Global Voices
Screenshot of X video of the October 10, 2026 protest in Quito, Ecuador. Video by X user Elena Rodríguez. Fair Use.

This post is part of Global Voices’ November 2026 Spotlight series, “Justice as infrastructure.” In this Spotlight, Global Voices is partnering with The Hague Institute for Innovation of Law (HiiL) to highlight the ways justice functions as critical infrastructure for any society. You can support this coverage by donating here.

In Quito, in defiance of the Jóvenes en Acción (Youth in Action) strategy with which Daniel Noboa’s government has attempted to boost employment for young people, thousands of students have been staging marches and sit-ins in streets and squares, demanding medicines, security, and a budget for education.

Their protests show a clear departure from the traditional approach to collective mobilization in Ecuador. Previously, these types of events have been led by the Confederation of Indigenous Nationalities of Ecuador (CONAIE); trade union groups such as the Ecuador Confederation of Free Trade Union Organizations (CEOSL), the United Workers’ Front (FUT), and the National Union of Educators (UNE); as well as feminist, anti-mining, and environmentalist movements.

However, on the afternoon of Saturday, October 10, 2026, the Ecuadorian capital witnessed a massive mobilization led by high school and university students, who gathered outside the Central University to march to Quito’s Historic Center. The call was made by the Autonomous Resistance Front (FARO), which comprises several youth collectives:
Lo que pasa en Quito es impresionante:

Quienes encabezaban la marcha anunciaron su finalización y llamaron a dispersarse. Sin embargo, la multitud continúa avanzando por las calles de Quito, desafiando el asedio policial y haciendo resonar consignas contra el Gobierno de Daniel Noboa. @teleSURtv
— Elena Rodríguez Yánez (@ElenaDeQuito) October 10, 2026

What is happening in Quito is striking: Those leading the march announced its conclusion and called for the crowd to disperse. Nevertheless, the throng continues to move through the streets of Quito, defying a police blockade and chanting slogans against the government of Daniel Noboa.

With their presence in the streets, the young people of Quito denounced the deterioration of public services, including the lack of medical supplies and medicines in hospitals, cuts to the public education budget, low youth employment, a persistent increase in insecurity, and forced disappearances at the hands of state agents. Their slogans also spoke out against the genocide in Palestine and the United States’ interventionism in Latin America.
Structural failures driving youth mobilization

According to figures from the National Institute of Statistics and Census (INEC), 40 percent of unemployed people in Ecuador are between 15 and 24 years old. Labor precariousness, a dearth of opportunities, and the high cost of living are just some of the factors affecting the country’s youth.

Meanwhile, on October 30, the Noboa administration launched its third edition of “Youth in Action,” an initiative aimed at the 18-29 demographic, who are promised temporary, two-month jobs with a salary of USD 400 per month. The measure has faced harsh criticism from various academics and civic sector representatives, who maintain that the absence of a comprehensive, long-term vision proves its inefficiency in tackling youth unemployment.

In November 2025, Ecuador’s National Assembly approved the country’s 2026 budget proposal, which hit public universities, polytechnic schools, co-financed institutions, and postgraduate programs with an allocated budget reduction of approximately USD 99 million. The decrease was reflected in the absence of student scholarships, non-existent investment in research, and a reduction in available slots to access free public higher education, which is established as a fundamental right in Article 26 of Ecuador’s Constitution.
Slogans as the language of youth resistance

During the peaceful youth march, participants chanted slogans like “Out Noboa, out,” “If the people have no peace, the government won’t either,” and “Noboa, fascist,” expressing indignation against a government they believe has failed to solve social problems that affect not only young people, but the majority of the population.

Direct rejection of deficient public administration, coupled with excessive state violence against citizens, motivated the students to protest. Many videos posted on social media captured police aggression against peaceful demonstrators, as well as physical assaults on journalists as they reported on the protests.
teleSUR reporter Elena Rodríguez Yánez shared her experience on X:

Estoy harta de tener que narrar, una y otra vez, las agresiones policiales contra la prensa. Hoy, mientras intentaba documentar la violencia con la que los agentes golpeaban a jóvenes manifestantes, recibí por la espalda un toletazo en la cabeza. I am fed up with having to recount, time and again, police assaults against the press. Today, while attempting to document the violence with which officers were beating young protesters, I was struck on the back of the head with a baton. I turned around and held up my teleSUR microphone to identify myself as a journalist; the response was another blow from a baton, which ended up shattering it.

We journalists do not want to be the news. I have no desire to be the protagonist of anything. I am out on the streets to report on what is happening — to document things that those in power would often prefer no one to see.

And if they think that by using force — by raining down blows — they can make me stop recording police brutality, force me to put away my microphone, or push me back several blocks so that I might practice journalism from a place where I won’t cause any ‘inconvenience,’ they are sorely mistaken.
It is not the journalists who should step away from the events; it is the police who must stop the assaults. The right to report cannot be negotiated at the end of a baton.
Hatari Ulcuango, President of the Federation of Students of the Catholic University of Ecuador, warned in one of his speeches that these mobilizations were “just the beginning.”

On October 10, as young people occupied the streets with their marches and sit-ins, they also used art to make their voices heard, singing songs, playing musical instruments, wearing masks, and dressing up in costumes. In doing so, they demonstrated that together, they can be very strong and that violence is not needed to speak one’s mind.

The government responded by sending the authorities to quell the protests and repress the demonstrators. Denunciations of the outcomes of state violence — dozens of students suffocated, injured, and detained — quickly spread across social media. These young people promised, however, that as long as they go unheard and continue to be treated with the blunt coercion of the state, they will return to the streets and not falter.

The leading role of youth in the streets of Ecuador, pitted against the state’s capacity for violent repression, evidence not only the crisis of the social state and the consolidation of an exclusionary state, but also the historical role of young people as agents of political change.

The glass generation — the one society has tried to shield — is experiencing the contradictions of an economic and political system that excludes them, making their future increasingly uncertain, and they are doing something about it.
Written by Gina Yauri
b8969565bb0ca4f9: When multinational companies decide where to build a factory, open a mine or establish a regional office, they have to consider whether the investment will still be profitable years into the future. Making that decision increasingly means thinking about risks, like whether surrounding roads will flood, worker safety will be compromised by extreme heat in the summer, and clean water will be available. As climate change increases the frequency and intensity of extreme weather events around the world, these effects can be especially severe in poorer countries that lack the resources to prepare for disasters or recover quickly after they hit. I study how political and environmental risks affect international business. In my new book, “Multinational Corporations and Climate Change: Risks, Responsibilities, and Resilience,” I explore how disaster risk is affecting the ways global companies see these climate-vulnerable markets, and how those views are leading some foreign investors to avoid these developing nations altogether. Low- and middle-income countries aren’t the only ones that suffer when multinational corporations pass them by. The companies themselves also stand to lose out on business opportunities in emerging markets if they pull away. How climate risk affects foreign investment Evidence from several studies suggests that multinationals are systematically avoiding investing in the most climate-vulnerable countries. These include my own analysis of 159 countries. Although these studies focus on different samples, they identify the same trend: Countries characterized by greater climate vulnerability received less foreign investment. The results are not trivial. My book identifies a 12% reduction in foreign direct investment for each 1-point rise in climate vulnerability on a 100-point scale, while holding other relevant factors constant. This vulnerability data measures countries’ exposure to climate hazards as well as their capacity to adapt. Companies rarely say why they’re avoiding a particular location, but their climate-related concerns occasionally become visible. For example, Google halted plans to build a US$200 million data center in Chile after an environmental court revoked its construction permit over the likely effects on water supplies and the environment. Similarly, a $1 billion data center proposed in Kenya by Microsoft and the Abu Dhabi-based artificial intelligence company G42 was delayed and ultimately suspended amid concerns about water stress in the area. Companies have reason to be cautious about climate risks. One analysis of 71 large publicly traded companies found that firms reporting major flood losses experienced a 5% average decline in shareholder value over the following year, after accounting for broader market movements. In Vietnam, typhoons and floods caused an estimated $475 million in damage to energy and transportation infrastructure in 2022. Unreliable infrastructure cost companies there about $280 million. An aerial view shows scores of vehicles submerged at a flooded Honda factory in Thailand in November 2011. Paula Bronstein /Getty Images Severe flooding in Thailand in 2011 forced several companies, including Toyota, Nissan and Honda, to temporarily suspend production as factories flooded, shutting down production of parts or vehicles made there. Costs like those shape where companies choose to invest next. While climate risk does not stop all investment in climate-vulnerable markets, it does make projects in these nations relatively more expensive, less attractive and more difficult to finance than less risky locations. Who loses from investor avoidance? For developing countries, less foreign investment means fewer jobs are created. These countries also have fewer opportunities to benefit from exposure to the new technologies that multinationals bring when they invest abroad. Those results highlight another way climate change is deepening global inequality. It reduces the economic activity that could support future development, while simultaneously damaging physical infrastructure and threatening human health and well-being. Developing countries are especially vulnerable to the effects of rising global temperatures, whether for their dependence on agricultural markets, geography or relatively fragile infrastructure. A report from the Climate Impact Lab at the University of Chicago projects that 90% of heat-related deaths in the coming decades will take place in low- and middle-income countries. Similarly, a 2022 study found that around 90% of people exposed to flooding live in developing nations. Yet poor countries have contributed only a tiny fraction of the emissions that are causing climate change, even as they face the brunt of the damage. For example, African countries are responsible for less than 4% of greenhouse gas emissions globally. But they stand to experience the greatest negative effects of climate change. Lost opportunities for multinational companies When a company avoids investing in climate-vulnerable countries, that may reduce its exposure to floods, droughts or extreme heat, but the decision also carries potential costs for the company. Many of these countries have growing consumer markets, energy resources or critical minerals that multinationals need. Companies that dismiss them as too risky may lose out on promising opportunities. For example, the Democratic Republic of Congo supplies most of the world’s cobalt, while Indonesia has become the dominant producer of nickel. These countries are highly vulnerable to climate change, which is likely scaring some companies away. Yet companies with a greater tolerance for risk have established strong positions in those countries’ mineral industries. Thus, more cautious firms may reduce their risk exposure, but they are also surrendering access to important resources and growing markets. Reducing investor avoidance There are ways to help companies overcome their climate-risk avoidance so more investment can pour into these countries: Foreign aid from wealthy countries can help developing countries shore up their roads, ports, electrical grids and water systems before extreme storms or droughts occur. My 2025 study found that climate-vulnerable countries that received more aid for climate adaptation also received more foreign direct investment than those receiving less aid. The result suggests the funding may reassure companies that climate risks are being addressed. International development banks can share some of the risks by providing climate risk insurance to multinationals. This would offer a safety net to absorb some of the losses if a covered disruption prevents a project from operating as intended. The World Bank already offers similar coverage against political risk incidents, which has given companies confidence to invest in countries such as Kenya, Mozambique and Nigeria. Better data can give companies more precise information about climate risks. Many risk scores label entire nations as vulnerable or not, even though exposure varies from one city or project site to another. More detailed information about local flood exposure, water availability, heat, infrastructure and adaptation capabilities would allow companies to limit their avoidance to the riskiest areas, instead of bypassing those countries altogether. Understanding the local risk, insuring companies against risk and helping countries make their infrastructure more resilient to storms, droughts and heat can help boost investment in ways that benefit the companies and spur economic growth and development in climate-vulnerable countries at the same time. 9ac3f87d0b7ef077: State efforts to tax the rich did relatively well in the 2026 midterm elections, following a series of state legislative moves in that direction in recent years. That might come as a surprise because a majority of voters rejected California’s Proposition 40. The much-publicized ballot initiative would have imposed a one-time 5% tax on the net worth of the state’s roughly 200 billionaires. Google co-founder Sergey Brin and several other billionaires spent nearly $400 million trying to persuade voters to reject it. Emmanuel Saez, a University of California, Berkeley economist who studies inequality and helped design Proposition 40, lamented the loss, saying: “Today oligarchy has won.” As a law professor who recently wrote a book about wealth inequality, I have been monitoring the results of these efforts aimed at taxing the rich. Despite Proposition 40’s failure, I think it’s important to observe that many Americans expressed support during the midterms for hiking income taxes on the rich, and to a lesser extent, taxes on the second – or third or fourth – homes the very wealthy possess. Taxing the rich at the ballot box Taxing income is proving a more successful strategy than taxing wealth. Major changes to income taxes were up for a vote in five states during the midterms. Three of those ballot initiatives were proposals that sought to boost income tax rates on the rich or maintain those rates. All three prevailed. In Washington state, for example, voters backed a measure that will preserve its new 9.9% income tax on household income above $1 million. This “millionaire’s tax,” signed into law earlier in 2026, is the state’s first personal income tax. Meanwhile, Colorado voters rejected Proposition 136, which would have capped the state’s income tax rate at 4.4%. They also approved Amendment 87, a new graduated income tax that raises rates on households and businesses with incomes over $500,000. And even though California’s voters rejected Proposition 40, they did approve Proposition 3. That measure makes permanent the income tax rates enacted in 2012 for the state’s highest earners, which were set to expire in 2031. The surcharges, adjusted annually for inflation, start at 10.3% for incomes of $360,000 and go up to a 12.3% surcharge for taxpayers earning over $721,000. And in August 2026, Missouri voters overwhelmingly rejected a measure that would have required the state’s lawmakers to eliminate its income tax. This would have meant losing $8.5 billion in revenue annually. The change would have let rich income taxpayers off the hook and replaced lost revenue through an increased sales tax that would have hit low-income taxpayers hardest. The two losses were in North Carolina and Iowa. Neither state voted directly on a tax to be levied on the rich. But both approved constitutional amendments that will make it harder for the state legislatures to enact these kinds of taxes in the future. North Carolina’s governor, Josh Stein, called the amendment in his state a “millionaire protection cap.” People visit the Billionaire Tax Now booth at the 2026 California Democratic Party State Convention in San Francisco, on Feb. 21, 2026, months before a ballot initiative that would have introduced such a measure failed to garner enough support. AP Photo/Jeff Chiu State legislatures raising income tax rates on high earners Ahead of the midterms, new taxes on the rich introduced via state legislatures, rather than ballot initiatives, also emerged. In Maine, legislators voted in April 2026 for a tax surcharge of 1% on income over $1 million. The following month, Hawaiian lawmakers created a new 13% income bracket for single taxpayers earning above $500,000 or couples filing jointly who make over $1 million. This change is paired with a reduction in rates for lower-income brackets. And one month after that, Rhode Island enacted a surcharge for millionaires’ income to be phased in over the next three years, reaching a maximum 3% rate. In 2009, New York became one of the first states to pass one of these high-earner income taxes. Washington, D.C., Massachusetts and Maryland also enacted these “millionaire taxes” in 2022, 2023 and 2025, respectively. Taxing additional homes Another way that state and local governments are boosting the tax revenue they get from wealthy constituents is by levying special taxes on pricey homes that aren’t the owners’ primary residences. These initiatives have succeeded both in state legislatures and voting booths. Montana lawmakers, in April 2025, approved a new tiered property tax system, which took effect on Jan. 1, 2026. It raised property tax rates on vacation homes and short-term rentals to 1.9%, while primary residences and qualifying long-term rentals pay lower, tiered homestead rates. New York City rolled out its “pied-à-terre tax” in July. The new tax imposes an annual surcharge of 0.8% to 1.3% on single-family homes valued at $5 million or more, and 4% to 6.5% on condos and co-ops valued at $1 million or more. The surcharge only applies to homes that are not a primary residence. Rhode Island has a similar property tax that took effect at the same time as New York City’s. It’s an annual surcharge of $2.50 for every $500 of assessed value above $1 million that applies to non-primary residences. And on Nov. 3, voters in Boulder, Colorado, approved a residential vacancy tax on homes that sit empty more than half the year. The surcharge, which goes into effect in 2028, will be roughly $4,000 a year for each vacant property. It applies across the board, but homes that aren’t primary residences are the clear target. However, just west of Boulder in Crested Butte, Colorado, a second-home tax failed. So did an effort to levy a similar surcharge in San Diego, California. New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani speaks about the fiscal year 2027 budget in New York City on May 12, 2026. Timothy A. Clary/AFP via Getty Images Why income taxes are attractive to voters and lawmakers There is a good reason why taxing the income of rich people is easier to pull off than taxing their wealth: Income taxes are much easier to calculate. Income taxes can be based on annual income tax filings, whether state or federal. It requires no extra work to value someone’s net worth. There are no such filings for wealth, except after death, if a large estate is left behind. Wealth taxes also require the annual valuation of businesses, farmland, artwork, intellectual property and other assets – many of which are hard to estimate. The downside of taxing income instead of wealth is that it limits how much revenue can be raised from the people most able to pay taxes. Most wealthy people convert little of their wealth into income. One common exception occurs when they sell some of their stock. Property taxes, like income taxes, are an exception to this rule. Calculating how much tax on real estate someone owes is easy for the authorities to do using annual municipal assessments. What might happen next? Despite Proposition 40’s defeat, it looks like Americans are generally open to taxing wealthy people more – at least when the states do it. In Illinois, where a billionaire governor, JB Pritzer, easily won a third term, another interesting ballot initiative prevailed. More than 75% of voters in Cook County, which includes Chicago and several of its suburbs, approved a nonbinding, advisory referendum asking if Illinois should adopt the “millionaire amendment for property tax relief and education.” It would levy a new surcharge of 3% on incomes over $1 million. While this win did not authorize a new tax, it revealed that support for one would be strong – at least in Chicago and Evanston. Even billionaire Bill Gates has said he believes a “billionaire’s tax” will be necessary. The question is: What kind? 59c5e44d58a3eccd: The first talks between Russia and Ukraine in nine months have concluded. The most positive thing that can be said about the US-mediated meeting in Abu Dhabi was that the dialogue did not break down and the parties seemed to agree to further meetings. There was also at least one tangible result. Russia and Ukraine agreed on a large-scale exchange of prisoners of war, the magnitude of which will be clarified over the coming days. Beyond this, however, there were few signs of progress towards a peace agreement. Despite Ukrainian president Volodymyr Zelensky’s claim that all participants in the negotiation process “genuinely want to achieve a result before 2027”, the most important issues remain unresolved. These include ceasefire terms, the future status of occupied regions and long-term security guarantees for Ukraine. The talks took place against the backdrop of continued fighting on the frontline. Russia’s military currently controls about a fifth of Ukraine, but progress on the battlefield has slowed in 2026 – and has even been reversed – due to Ukrainian successes. With the frontline largely static, Moscow keeps striking Ukrainian cities and energy sites with missiles and drones. In turn, Ukraine has attacked Russian oil refineries and other energy infrastructure. The Russian military currently controls a fifth of Ukrainian territory. Institute for the Study War According to reports from Abu Dhabi, Ukraine firmly rejected a proposal for it to surrender the entire Donbas region in the east of the country in return for peace. Whether the Russian demand for the Donbas indicates a softening of its claim to the Kherson and Zaporizhzhia regions remains too early to determine. The deadlock remains on other key issues, too. Russia continues to insist that a restructuring of Europe’s security architecture must be put in place before any ceasefire can take effect, to address what it regards as its legitimate security concerns. On the eve of its full-scale invasion in 2022, Russia demanded the withdrawal of Nato forces from countries that joined the alliance after 1997. These include the Czech Republic, Hungary, Poland and other eastern European states. If this demand still stands, it is difficult to envisage an end to the war anytime soon. Ukraine, for its part, is bracing itself for another harsh winter. It therefore seeks a ceasefire as the starting point for any serious negotiations on peace. This demand, backed by its European supporters, has so far fallen on deaf ears in the Kremlin. This was evidenced by missile strikes that continued even during the peace talks themselves. The coercive nature of Russia’s strategy was further underlined by the fact that six major electricity substations in central Ukraine were reportedly struck during the night between the two days of negotiations. Perhaps the most important new point of departure for the Abu Dhabi talks was a new initiative by the Trump administration to tie a peace deal to a broader European security framework. US envoy Jared Kushner, the son-in-law of President Donald Trump, has said this framework would provide security guarantees to Ukraine while also meeting Russian security demands. The details of what such a construction would look like are hidden from the public view. But if the recent stances of the Trump administration are of any guidance, those details are likely to be closer to Russian preferences than Ukrainian ones. In recent weeks, Trump has struck a controversial deal that has allowed Moscow to restore some of its diesel exports, waiving several sanctions in the process. Steve Witkoff, another US presidential envoy, also praised Russian leader Vladimir Putin as a “humanitarian” in late October. Left in the cold So far, the deep irony seems to be that while the issue of a broader European security architecture is on the table, the European countries supporting Ukraine are denied a place at the negotiating table itself. Even though there were representatives of the EU, Nato, France, Germany, Italy and the UK present in Abu Dhabi, they were not given formal voice in the negotiating process. On the first day of the meeting, Russian foreign minister Sergei Lavrov even sarcastically joked about letting them sit there in their hotels. If the US continues to scale down its military presence in Europe, as Trump has repeatedly hinted it will, responsibility for providing the security guarantees Ukraine will so desperately need after the war will fall largely on the EU and European Nato members. This would again call for giving Europe a voice and presence at the negotiating table, which seems to have been recognised at least by Kushner. After the Abu Dhabi talks concluded, he was reported as saying European partners must be at the table in future rounds. He said he would raise the matter with Putin. Europe’s participation in the talks is not a marginal issue, particularly as the position of the US as an honest broker has become debatable, given the tendency of the Trump administration to side with Russia on essential issues. Trump’s recent remark that Ukraine might “end up with a little bit different shape” after the war suggests this remains the case. The Abu Dhabi meeting has at least revived negotiations between the two warring parties. But it is far from evident that peace has moved any closer. The most contentious issues remain essentially where they were before the parties convened in the Emirates. Bo Petersson receives funding from Malmö University and the Hamrin Foundation.

b5a7a069ea875674: There is a long list of people who have been, or still are, under detention in their own homes around the world.
Many are former heads of state or government. Apart from Najib Razak, we can count Myanmar’s Aung San Suu Kyi and former French president Nicolas Sarkozy among them.
Like Najib, Sarkozy was convicted of a criminal offence. On the other hand, Suu Kyi is being detained for her opposition to the military dictatorship that continues to hold sway in Myanmar.
Another politician who also lived at home but as a prisoner was ex-Argentine president Cristina Fernández de Kirchner.
Unlike Malaysia, both Argentina and France already had provisions in their legal systems for home detention when their respective leaders — in this instance de Kirchner and Sarkozy — were sentenced.

In Argentina, the provision for house arrest goes back a long way — all the way back to 1886 when its first National Criminal Code was put in place. There have been several updates — in 1921, 1996 and subsequently in 2008.
According to Argentina.gob.ar, the official portal of the Argentine State, several conditions must be met before a prisoner qualifies for home detention.
He or she must be suffering from a terminal illness, or a malady that “cannot be adequately treated in prison” but does not require hospitalisation.
A person with a disability, making him vulnerable to inhumane or degrading treatment in a prison environment or any person aged over 70 also qualifies. So do pregnant women and caregiving mothers.
At age 72, de Kirchner qualifies on age alone.
In France, house arrest is provided for under Article 142-5 of the French Code of Criminal Procedure.

It states that a person convicted of a criminal offence and sentenced to a year or less in jail can be confined to his home under strict conditions. The prisoner must also show that he does not pose a flight risk.
Sarkozy was sentenced to three years but qualified anyway because two of those three years were suspended.
As far as we know, Najib is neither ill nor pregnant. He does not have any young child to watch over either.
At age 76, former Negeri Sembilan menteri besar Isa Samad is still serving out his six-year prison sentence for corruption. Najib is three years younger than him.
Even if we pick a leaf or two from the Argentine and French playbooks on home detention, Najib does not qualify on any front.

In September, Najib was granted a conditional pardon by the Yang di-Pertuan Agong under which he could serve out the remainder of his six-year sentence in the SRC International case under house arrest.
The condition was that he paid the RM50 million fine. Umno managed to raise the sum and the fine was paid on Nov 6.
Najib is already home to continue serving his sentence, but it is not too late to start thinking about putting in place provisions for house arrest.
Chances are there will be more to come.

a865d7bae4f04a4d: Accurate, up-to-date climate projections are essential for planning decisions that enhance the resilience of power grids, protect public health, maximize agricultural yields, and more. Now, MIT researchers have developed a technique that streamlines the production of fast, trustworthy, and adaptable artificial intelligence models for climate prediction. These specialized AI models, known as climate emulators, can rapidly simulate the effects of human activities onto a future climate, predicting impacts on temperatures or sea level, for example.  Because emulators run in a matter of seconds, scientists use them to efficiently test thousands of varied climate scenarios. This provides more reliable estimates and can identify unexpected outcomes of regional interventions. The MIT researchers developed a training technique that boosts the performance and adaptability of a climate emulator while using only a fraction of the data typically required. This significantly cuts production time for these practical scientific tools. They show that an emulator trained with a much smaller amount of carefully selected synthetic data accurately predicts outcomes of scenarios it did not see during training, while traditional emulators failed to adapt to new situations. “Climate emulators are especially well-suited for modeling policy-relevant scenarios. By using our method to generate optimized training data for an emulator, we can speed up the production of much more reliable emulators, so we can better trust their outputs for making policy decisions,” says Christoher Womack PhD ’26, who is now a postdoc at ETH Zurich and lead author of a paper on this technique. He is joined on the paper by Shahine Bouabid, a postdoc in the MIT Department of Earth, Atmospheric and Planetary Sciences (EAPS); Andrei Sokolov, a research scientist in MIT’s Center for Sustainability Science and Strategy (CS3); Popat Salunke, a postdoc in CS3; Glenn Flierl, a professor of oceanography in EAPS; Sebastian D. Eastham, an associate professor at Imperial College London; and senior author Noelle E. Selin, a professor in the MIT Institute for Data, Systems, and Society (IDSS) and EAPS, and director of CS3. The research appears this week in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences.  Speedier surrogates Climate scientists typically use earth system models (ESMs) to make long-term projections about how global temperature or precipitation could change in response to varying greenhouse gas emissions. These enormous, physics-based models capture the major components and interactions of the earth’s climate in extreme detail. While powerful, ESMs can take months to run on a cluster of supercomputers — and that’s only to project one possible future climate scenario.  Selin and her collaborators design climate emulators, which are fast AI surrogate models that mimic the behavior of full-scale ESMs. Emulators help scientists test many scenarios, make more accurate forecasts, and explore specific pollutants and regional effects. “Climate emulators can run in just a few seconds, so it really expands what we can do in terms of exploring these future climate scenarios,” Womack says. When scientists design a climate emulator, they often train the AI model using a set of six to eight future scenarios based on realistic future trajectories of emissions. They must run each scenario through a full-scale ESM, making these datasets costly and time-consuming to generate.  The MIT researchers recently found that using realistic future scenarios as training data can lead to underperforming emulators that fail to predict unfamiliar or novel scenarios.  In this work, they developed an algorithm that generates a synthetic dataset of optimized climate scenarios tailored to boost one emulator’s predictive performance. “Our algorithm might generate some weird scenarios which look nothing like a realistic future, but we don’t care so much if the training scenarios are realistic. We are just trying to make the best possible dataset to train an emulator,” Womack says. Importantly, rather than needing to run a full ESM six or eight times to generate training data, a user would only need to run that model once. Tuning the training data  The researchers begin by generating an arbitrary climate scenario using a fast and simple climate model. They test how well their emulator can reproduce the results of that ESM, which gives them a measure of error. Because of the programming technique they used to build the training pipeline, they can iteratively update the training data to increase the emulator’s predictive skill. For instance, the algorithm could increase CO2 emissions dramatically in the year 2050 or rapidly decrease methane emissions in 2037. Then the optimization updates the training data until the emulator’s error level reaches a certain threshold. In the end, rather than resembling realistic scenarios in which emissions follow smooth trajectories, the synthetic data contain rapid variations. “By introducing these high-frequency wiggles and oscillations, our data enable the emulator to extract a lot more information about the overall system,” Womack explains. Their training algorithm outputs these emissions scenarios, which they can use to train an emulator that is more accurate and adaptable. “In the future, we are definitely going to see climates and scenarios we haven’t seen before. If we can simulate these different scenarios more robustly, we can provide more reliable information to the stakeholders who need it,” Selin says. For instance, an emulator trained with their technique can capture the effects of local pollutant control policies that reduce one pollutant while other emissions continue rising. The traditional emulators they evaluated failed this test.   In the long run, Womack hopes this work improves the usefulness of fast and adaptable climate emulators for policy formulation.  “This is such an important piece of the pipeline when it comes to creating useful tools that speak to stakeholder needs. Because the process of training an emulator can takes months or even years, the emulators we have are usually out-of-date. By cutting down that production time, I think this technique will be a game-changer in terms of getting updated tools into the hands of researchers and practitioners,” Selin adds. In the future, the researchers want to test their technique using an emissions scenario generated by a full ESM. They also want to apply it to other types of climate models and explore its effectiveness in broader machine learning and computer vision applications. This research was part of the Bringing Computation to the Climate Challenge (BC3) project and supported by Schmidt Sciences through the MIT Grand Challenges.
474f4a5c982096f4: Since the October 2023 Hamas attack on Israel, and during Israel’s now three-year-long retaliation against Gaza, journalism’s traditional commitment to objectivity has been on trial. Reporting on the Israel–Gaza war has been characterised, on social media as much as in the conservative media, as biased one way or the other. Headlines have been parsed and corrected by social media warriors while a war of words between new journalism players and traditional media has been loud and often angry. This clash has emphasised the tension between the objective reporting claimed to be practiced by legacy media and advocacy-oriented reporting that internet journalists believe delivers more truth. In contrast, the Russian military attack on Ukraine has been reported with milder popular criticism. The privileging of one side’s narrative over the other in this conflict appears not to have attracted the same claims of media bias. Numerous studies have shown trust declines when audiences perceive journalism to be advocating for one position over another. In addition, they have a marked preference for news that incorporates a range of views. This led the Centre for Media Transition to examine the way Australian media have framed both international conflicts. Reporting in conflict We sought to understand if particular narratives have been privileged over others and if so, how. It is a normal part of the reporting process for journalists to decide what information to include, omit, emphasise, and contextualise in order to report a story. This framing process allows journalists to make some narratives more dominant and decide what sources are used to support them. On top of framing there is journalistic voice. Despite the best efforts of a reporter to achieve objectivity, this can often be evaluative or subjective. We examined the framing choices made by The Australian, the ABC, 9News.com.au, and The Guardian across the two conflicts when the events being reported were significant in the news cycle. We gauged how each dealt with the dominant narratives emerging from the main parties to the conflicts. We also looked at which voices were given more space, whose stories were personalised or depersonalised, and which contemporary and historical contexts were prioritised or deprioritised. Whose story is being told? Our results show the media outlets across the 2023–2026 events we looked at, shifted their framing between Israeli and Palestinian narratives, depending on events on the ground. Despite the movement in framing, Israeli frames emerged as dominant overall in 49% of surveyed articles against 32% with Palestinian narratives. All the surveyed media outlets engaged closely with Israeli narratives following the October 7 2023 Hamas assault. But as the Palestinian death toll increased and events in Gaza raised alarm bells, the ABC, 9News.com.au, and The Guardian amplified the humanitarian consequences to the Palestinians (Palestinian frames comprised 38%, 27%, and 54% of their respective samples), although the volume of the coverage was smaller. These outlets continued reporting Israeli security concerns as counterclaims while centring Palestinian victimhood until the conflict escalated to involve the US, Iran, Lebanon, and the Gulf states. Only The Australian continued to privilege Israeli perspectives across all surveyed events. The masthead emphasised Israel’s narratives of victimhood, security, and self-defence (71% of the total outlet’s sample adopted Israeli frames as dominant). It also marginalised Palestinian narratives (3% of The Australian’s overall sample used Palestinian frames), including the history of this long and frequently brutal conflict. The Australian was also the only outlet to align pro-Palestinian advocacy in Australia with narratives of antisemitism and social division. It criticised the Greens for the party’s vociferous support for the Palestinians. It also aligned the most radical of pro-Palestinian voices with more moderate ones, particularly around the time of Australia’s recognition of Palestinian statehood in the UN. Ukraine conflict tells a different story In coverage of the Russia–Ukraine war between 2022–2026, our results show a very different use of journalistic framing. We found an asymmetry in engagement with and treatment of the narratives emerging from both sides. Western and Ukrainian narratives were continuously dominant across 67% of the sampled coverage by all four outlets surveyed, and the voices given prominence were overwhelmingly Western and Ukrainian. Russian narratives received almost no interpretive authority. In fact, in the articles we surveyed, 0% engaged with Russian frames as dominant. Indeed, when Russian frames were referenced to understand what Russia still calls a “special military operation” rather than war, it was mostly to disparage them. As a result, historical and geopolitical complexity of post-Soviet foreign policy was significantly downplayed. This includes Russian arguments that NATO’s eastward expansion in Europe was threatening, and Russia did not view NATO as a defence alliance. One strong strain of reporting was that Russian president Vladimir Putin was an irrational actor, and his war on Ukraine indicated a psychological malaise. Another was that Russia was paradoxically threatening yet internally fragile, economically weak yet able to survive global sanctions, unable to conquer Ukraine yet able to wage war against Europe. In this conflict, to a far greater extent than in Israel–Gaza reporting, evaluative journalistic voice was apparent. This portrayed the war through a historical lens of Soviet and Russian expansionism, while references to the controversial Minsk Agreements were largely left unexplored. While source privileging and selective framing are the hallmark of advocacy journalism, this does not necessarily mean a piece of reporting is advocacy. Sometimes, there is broad consensus in support of one side and in opposition to the other – as there is in relation to Russia’s war on Ukraine. In contrast, there are polarised responses around Israel–Gaza, where violations of international humanitarian law against Palestinians and Israel during the Hamas attack were documented. But the journalistic obligation to analyse and engage viewpoints with which journalists may not agree or accept does not simply disappear in the practice of objective journalism. The obligation can disappear in the practice of advocacy journalism such that one side’s interpretation becomes embedded as a default perspective. But the question then becomes whether this is actually journalism. In 2022, Professor Attard was formally banned from entering Russia for what the Kremlin labelled a “Russophobia agenda”. Alena Radina is a Russian citizen.
01fe3273792f42dd: Ada satu pesona di rak buku ibu yang memikat dan menawan saya iaitu karya Raja Ali Haji, dengan judul Gurindam Dua Belas yang dipercayai dikarang atau tersebar sekitar tahun 1847.

Apa yang menyebabkan saya suka dengan gurindam adalah kerana ia tiada tentu bentuknya. Ia boleh jadi terikat atau tidak. Untuk gurindam dengan bentuk yang terikat, ia terdiri dari dua baris serangkap, mengandungi tiga hingga enam perkataan sebaris dengan rima a-a. Beberapa rangkap berkait akan menjadikan ia satu gagasan atau idea yang boleh dicerna. Sudah tentu Gurindam Dua Belas tersebut memukau saya.

Apabila saya menuliskan novel saya dengan tajuk Koro; salah satu pengikat atau pesona kepada karya ini dibina menerusi gurindam. Koro yang diterbitkan di Indonesia oleh Penerbit Circa pada tahun 2022, dan kemudian diterjemahkan ke bahasa Inggeris oleh Brigitte Bresson, dan diterbitkan oleh Penguin Random House sebagai The Koro Riots (2023) mengisahkan sebuah negara fiksional Republik Hujung Manani yang dilanda penyakit koro iaitu kaum lelakinya mengalami pengecutan alat kelamin mendadak. Sebagai sebuah satira politik, saya cuba mengungkapkan punca korupsi dan kemerosotan moral warga di republik itu dan bagaimana usaha-usaha protagonisnya Negarawan Sejati menegakkan keadilan dan melaksanakan reformasi.

Untuk meyakinkan khalayak akan kewujudan sebuah negara imaginasi ini saya menciptakan lagu kebangsaan, sejarahnya yang pernah ditakluk Perancis, memerikan sosiopolitik dan ekonomi, garis sempadan, dan paling penting negara ini juga memiliki warisan budaya sendiri iaitu gurindam.

Di republik fiksi ini, Gurindam Enam dikenali dan dihafal oleh rakyatnya. Gurindam Enam memerihalkan enam pasal yang mesti diambil kira oleh sesebuah negara untuk kekal merdeka, selamat hala tujunya dan terpelihara dari serangan musuh.

Sudah tentu saya sendiri tidak dapat menjelaskan bagaimanakah ilham atau idea Gurindam Enam ini datang mengalir, melainkan ia terbangun daripada bacaan lampau, perenungan yang bertahun-tahun dahulu disentak oleh karya-karya tradisional yang unggul. Dalam erti kata lain, minda saya secara separuh sedar ketika mengarang Koro dalam tahun 2000 ke 2022 itu melilau dan menerawang di galaksi atau cakerawala fikir yang luas. Di dalam gurindam ini, saya mengungkapkan keseluruhan idea dan gagasan akal budi Melayu, dengan pesan besar bahawa terdapatnya musuh atau ancaman terhadap bangsa yang terdiri dalam bentuk pemerintah yang jahat, dan berpihak kepada yang korup; ulama yang tidak lagi menobatkan kebenaran dan keadilan; rakyat atau warga dilalaikan dengan candu dan madat; serta terakhir kumpulan saudagar kapitalis mementingkan haloba perut berbanding kesejahteraan umat.
Empat kelompok atau golongan yang menentukan arah baik dan buruknya negara ini bukanlah sesuatu yang boleh muncul secara tiba-tiba tentunya. Ia tiba dengan memori berjejak di dalam benak saya.
Enam pasal ingatan dalam gurindam ini dapat direnung dan dicermin kembali dalam pelbagai titah diraja oleh raja-raja Melayu.

Sebagai contoh tuntutan keadilan dan pesan agar raja sentiasa terpandu dinasihati, yang mana dalam konteks zaman moden kita di Malaysia adalah raja berpelembagaan sejajar dengan titah baginda Tuanku Muhriz Tuanku Munawir, Yang Dipertuan Besar Negeri Sembilan di Istiadat Pengurniaan Darjah Kebesaran, Bintang dan Pingat sempena Hari Keputeraan ke-78 baginda di Istana Besar Seri Menanti pada 14 Jan 2026.

"Rasuah merupakan musuh utama kepada keadilan, amanah dan masa depan negara. Beta amat terperanjat dan kecewa apabila masih wujud pihak yang terus memberikan sokongan kepada individu yang telah disabitkan bersalah atas tuduhan rasuah yang amat besar, seolah-olah perbuatan tersebut boleh diterima dan dimaafkan. Mereka yang masih menyokong penjenayah seperti ini agar segera bermuhasabah diri serta menilai semula pendirian dan kepercayaan masing-masing. Ini kerana sebarang bentuk toleransi atau kompromi terhadap rasuah adalah bertentangan dengan prinsip kebenaran, keadilan serta amanah dan sama sekali tidak boleh diterima dalam sebuah negara yang menjunjung kedaulatan undang-undang."

Tuanku Muhriz berasa khuatir sebarang toleransi dan kelonggaran kepada penjenayah dan jenayah rasuah boleh menjejaskan masa depan negara kita di mana keadilan dilihat tidak lagi dilaksanakan dengan setara, atau terdapat dwistandard antara kelas tertentu.

Baginda tidaklah bersendirian dalam menolak rasuah dan perasuah. Pada 22 Sept 2022 misalnya; Sultan Perak, Sultan Nazrin Muizzuddin Shah bertitah, ketika melancarkan buku tulisan M Kamal Hassan bertajuk 'Korupsi dan Kemunafikan Dalam Politik Melayu, Perlunya Disegerakan Transformasi Moral Etika', bahawa rasuah dikenal pasti sebagai salah satu sebab utama yang membantutkan pertumbuhan ekonomi, menghilangkan minat pelaburan asing, meningkatkan kos pentadbiran dan urus niaga, menidakkan rakyat daripada mendapat perkhidmatan, serta mendorong berlakunya ketidakstabilan politik.

Ingatan yang lebih jelas daripada Sultan Nazrin terpancar dalam titah baginda yang lebih mutakhir iaitu pada 2023, ketika Istiadat Menghadap Sembah Taat Setia dan Penganugerahan Darjah Kebesaran Negeri Perak Darul Ridzuan sempena sambutan Ulang Tahun Hari Keputeraan ke-66. Titah Sultan Nazrin lagi rakyat semakin lantang mendedahkan isu rasuah, gigih menolak pemimpin berimej rasuah dan menggunakan jawatan untuk kepentingan diri, atau pemimpin yang mengumpul kekayaan untuk ahli keluarga serta pemimpin yang menjadi instrumen kepada ahli perniagaan.

Saya mengimpikan Gurindam Enam akan menjadi sepertinya Gurindam Dua Belas, sebagai sebuah karya klasik yang bertahan zaman dan dihayati gagasan keseluruhannya seperti mana rakyat Hujung Manani lakukan di dalam novel Koro.
